p.seg: After Huáng Cháo died,
Qín Zōngquán declared himself emperor,
and captured Shǎn, Luò, Huái, Mèng, Táng, Xǔ, Rǔ, and Zhèng prefectures.
He dispatched his generals Qín Xián, Lú Táng, and Zhāng Ào to attack Biàn.
Xián's army was at Bǎnqiáo,
Ào's army was in the northern suburbs,
and Táng's army was at Wànshèng.
They encircled Biàn with thirty-six stockades.
The King, seeing his troops were few,
dared not sally forth.
So he sent Zhū Zhēn to recruit soldiers in the east,
and sought aid from Yǎn and Yùn.
In the spring of the third year,
Zhēn returned with ten thousand men and several hundred horses.
He then attacked Xián at Bǎnqiáo,
capturing four of his stockades.
He also attacked Táng at Wànshèng;
Táng was defeated
and threw himself into the water and died.
When Zōngquán heard of Táng and others' defeat,
he personally led several thousand elite soldiers
and set up a stockade in the northern suburbs.
In the fifth month,
Zhū Jǐn of Yǎnzōu and Zhū Xuān of Yùnzhōu came to provide aid.
The King held a feast in the army camp.
In the middle of the feast,
the King ostensibly rose to go to the latrine,
and with light troops, sallied out from the northern gate to raid Ào,
while the music did not stop.
Ào did not expect the arrival of the troops,
and the Yǎn and Yùn armies then joined in the attack,
completely defeating them,
beheading more than twenty thousand.
Zōngquán and Ào fled by night,
passing through Zhèng,
they massacred its city before leaving.
Zōngquán reached Cài,
and again sent Zhāng Ào to attack Biàn.
When the King heard Ào was returning,
he ascended the ridge behind Fēngchán Sì,
observed Ào's troops passing,
and sent Zhū Zhēn to follow them,
cautioning him:
"When Ào sees our troops,
he will surely stop.
When you see him stop,
you should return quickly,
do not fight him."
Soon after, Ào saw Zhēn behind him,
and indeed stopped.
Zhēn immediately galloped back.
The King ordered Zhēn to lead his troops to hide behind a large forest,
and he himself led elite cavalry out from its east,
lying in ambush between large mounds.
Ào stopped and ate.
After eating,
he raised his banners
and galloped to attack Zhēn.
Zhēn's troops retreated a little,
then the King led his hidden troops to emerge from the side,
cutting Ào's army into three and attacking them.
Ào was greatly defeated
and escaped.
Zōngquán was enraged
and beheaded Ào.
The troops from Héyáng, Shǎn, and Luò who were guarding for Zōngquán,
hearing that all of Cài's elite soldiers had been annihilated at Biàn,
then dispersed.
Therefore, Zhūgě Shuǎng's general Lǐ Hǎnzhī took Héyáng, and Zhāng Quányì took Luòyáng and came to submit.
In the tenth month,
the Son of Heaven sent an envoy,
bestowing upon the King a stele commemorating his achievements.
Zhū Xuān and Zhū Jǐn's armies, after assisting Biàn
and defeating Zōngquán, returned east.
The King then sent a manifesto to Yǎn and Yùn,
falsely accusing them of enticing Biàn's runaway soldiers to the east,
and then dispatched troops to attack them,
capturing their Cáo Prefecture and Pú Prefecture.
He then sent Zhū Zhēn to attack Yùnzhōu,
but he was greatly defeated and returned.
In the twelfth month,
the Son of Heaven sent an envoy,
bestowing upon the King an iron certificate and a stele of virtuous governance.
Initially, he was referred to by name;
later, by his noble title;
later still, he was referred to as emperor;
this was a gradual process.
It was only after reaching the title of King that he was referred to as such,
indicating his imminent rise.
It is customary in the common usage that
"Xuān"
follows
"Wáng"
is incorrect.
After Huáinán Jìdùshǐ Gāo Pián died,
Yáng Xíngmì entered Yángzhōu.
The Son of Heaven appointed the King concurrently as Huáinán Jìdùshǐ.
The King then memorialized Yáng Xíngmì as Deputy Envoy,
and appointed Xíngjūn Sīmǎ Lǐ Fán as Acting Governor (Liúhòu).
When Fán went to Yángzhōu,
Xíngmì did not receive him.
In the first month of Wéndé First Year,
the King went to Huáinán,
reaching Sòngzhōu and then returned.
At this time,
Qín Zōngquán captured Xiāngzhōu,
and appointed Zhào Déyīn as Jìdùshǐ.
Déyīn rebelled against Zōngquán and came to submit.
The Son of Heaven then appointed the King as Càizhōu Sìmiàn Xíngyíng Dūtǒng,
with Déyīn as his deputy.
On the Gēngzǐ day of the third month,
Xīzōng died.
Tiānxíong Jūn rebelled,
imprisoning their Jìdùshǐ Lè Yànzhēn.
His son, Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Cóngxùn, attacked Wèi
and came to request troops.
Zhū Zhēn was dispatched to assist Cóngxùn in attacking Wèi.
However, the Wèi army killed Yànzhēn,
Cóngxùn died in battle,
the Wèi people enthroned Luó Hóngxìn,
so Zhēn returned.
Zhāng Quányì took Héyáng,
expelling Lǐ Hǎnzhī.
Hǎnzhī fled to Hédōng.
Lǐ Kèyòng sent troops to besiege Héyáng,
Quányì came to seek aid.
Dīng Huì and Niú Cúnjié were dispatched to rescue him,
defeating the Hédōng troops at Yǎnhé.
In the fifth month,
the Xíngyíng attacked Càizhōu,
besieging it for over a hundred days,
but failed to capture it.
At this time,
Shí Pǔ had already been appointed Dōngnánmiàn Dūtǒng,
and the King was again appointed to command the Xíngyíng while Pǔ still retained the title of Dūtǒng.
The King then submitted a memorial,
arguing that Pǔ had achieved nothing in attacking Cài and yet had not lost his Dūtǒng title,
also intending to provoke Pǔ to initiate military action.
Earlier,
when Gāo Pián died,
Huáinán fell into chaos.
Chǔzhōu Cìshǐ Líu Zàn came to defect,
and was accepted.
When the King's forces attacked Cài unsuccessfully,
they returned,
intending to attack Xú.
So Zhū Zhēn was dispatched with several thousand troops to the east,
ostensibly to escort Zàn back to Chǔzhōu.
Pǔ was angered by the criticism of himself,
and upon hearing that Zhēn was coming with troops,
indeed sent out troops to resist him.
Zhēn fought at Wúkāng,
greatly defeating them,
and took their two counties of Fēng and Xiāo.
He then attacked Sùzhōu
and captured it.
Zhēn garrisoned Xiāoxiàn,
and separately sent Páng Shīgǔ to attack Xúzhōu.
In the first month of Lóngjì First Year,
Shīgǔ defeated Pǔ at Lǚliáng.
Huáixī Yájiàng Shēn Cóng captured Qín Zōngquán,
broke his legs,
and was about to cage him and send him to the capital;
another general Guō Fán killed Cóng,
usurped Zōngquán, and offered him (as a captive).
The King sent Xíngjūn Sīmǎ Lǐ Fán to present the captive to the capital,
and memorialized Guō Fán as Huáixī Liúhòu.
In the third month,
the Son of Heaven enfeoffed the King as Dōngpíng Wáng.
In the seventh month,
Zhū Zhēn killed Lǐ Tángbīn.
The King went to Xiāoxiàn,
seized Zhēn and killed him,
and then attacked Xúzhōu.
In winter,
there was heavy rain
and floods,
so he could not campaign and returned.
Initially,
Qín Zōngquán sent his younger brother Zōnghéng to plunder territory in Huáinán.
In this year,
Zōnghéng was killed by his general Sūn Rú,
and Rú attacked Yáng Xíngmì at Yángzhōu.
Huáinán fell into great chaos,
Xíngmì fled to Xuānzhōu,
and Rú entered Yángzhōu.
In the spring of Dàshùn First Year,
Páng Shīgǔ was dispatched to attack Sūn Rú in Huáinán,
but was greatly defeated and returned.
In the fourth month,
Sùzhōu general Zhāng Yún returned Sùzhōu to Shí Pǔ.
The King personally led an attack on it,
but failed to capture it.
In the twelfth year,
the Wèizhōu (魏州) army mutinied.
Hè Délún (賀德倫) rebelled against Liáng (梁) with Wèi (魏) and Bó (博) prefectures and defected.
The Wáng (王) entered Wèizhōu (魏州).
When he reached Yǒngjì (永濟),
he executed Zhāng Yàn (張彥), the leader of the mutiny,
and took his five hundred soldiers as his personal guards,
calling them the Zhàngqián Yínqiāng Jūn (帳前銀槍軍) (Silver Spear Army of the Tent).
In the sixth month,
the Wáng (王) concurrently held the title of Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Wèibó (魏博).
Dézhōu (德州) was taken.
In the seventh month,
Chánzhōu (澶州) was taken.
Liú Kuài (劉●) encamped at Huánshuǐ (洹水).
The Wáng (王) led one hundred cavalry to scout his camp.
He encountered Kuài's (●) ambushers, who surrounded him in several layers.
He broke through the encirclement,
losing seven or eight cavalrymen.
In the eighth month,
Liáng (梁) retook Chánzhōu (澶州).
The Jìn (晉) army and Kuài (●) faced each other at Shēn (莘).
The Jìn (晉) army repeatedly challenged them,
but Kuài (●) remained behind his fortifications.
In the first month of the thirteenth year,
the Wáng (王) left Lǐ Cúnshěn (李存審) at Shēn (莘),
announcing his intention to return west.
When Kuài (●) heard that the Jìn Wáng (晉王) was about to leave,
he immediately led his troops to attack Wèi (魏),
attacking the east of the city.
The Wáng (王), having reached Bèizhōu (貝州),
turned back to attack Kuài (●),
soundly defeating him.
He pursued him to Gù Yuánchéng (故元城),
defeated him again,
and Kuài (●) fled to Líyáng (黎陽).
In the third month,
he attacked Liáng's (梁) Wèizhōu (衞州),
and its Cìshǐ (刺史) Mǐ Zhāo (米昭) surrendered.
Cízhōu (磁州) was captured,
and its Cìshǐ (刺史) Jìn Zhāo (靳昭) was killed.
In the fourth month,
Míngzhōu (洺州) was captured.
In the eighth month,
Xíngzhōu (邢州) was besieged,
and its Jìedùshǐ (節度使) Yán Bǎo (閻寶) surrendered.
Zhāng Jūn (張筠) of Liáng (梁) abandoned Xiàngzhōu (相州) and Dài Sīyuǎn (戴思遠) abandoned Cāngzhōu (滄州) and fled.
The two prefectures were then taken.
The people of Bèizhōu (貝州) killed the Liáng (梁) commandant Zhāng Yuándé (張源德)
and surrendered the city.
The Qìdān (契丹) raided Wèizhōu (蔚州),
capturing Zhènwǔ Jìedùshǐ (振武節度使) Lǐ Sìběn (李嗣本).
In the fourteenth year,
the Qìdān (契丹) raided Xīnzhōu (新州),
and then Yōuzhōu (幽州).
Lǐ Sìyuán (李嗣源) attacked and drove them away.
In winter,
Xiè Yànzhāng (謝彥章) of Liáng (梁) encamped at Yángliú (楊劉).
In the twelfth month,
Yángliú (楊劉) was attacked.
The Wáng (王) personally carried fodder to fill the moats,
and thus breached it.
In the first month of the fifteenth year,
Liáng (梁) and Jìn (晉) confronted each other at Yángliú (楊劉).
Yànzhāng (彥章) diverted the river water to separate the Jìn (晉) army.
In the sixth month,
they crossed the water to attack Yànzhāng (彥章),
destroying four of his camps.
In the eighth month,
a grand review was held at Wèi (魏).
The armies of Lúlóng (盧龍), Hénghǎi (橫海), Zhāoyì (昭義), Ānguó (安國), as well as Zhèn (鎮) and Dìng (定), totaling one hundred thousand men and ten thousand horses, were assembled.
They encamped at Májiādù (麻家渡).
Xiè Yànzhāng (謝彥章) encamped at Xíngtái (行臺).
In the twelfth month,
the army advanced to Línpú (臨濮).
The Liáng (梁) army pursued them,
and they battled at Húliǔ (胡柳).
The Jìn (晉) army suffered a great defeat,
and Zhōu Déwēi (周德威) died.
The Liáng (梁) army rested at dusk on a dirt mound.
The Jìn (晉) army attacked again,
soundly defeating them.
They then encamped at Déshèng (德勝),
forming a double stockade.
In the first month of the sixteenth year,
the Wáng (王) concurrently held the title of Lúlóng Jūn Jìedùshǐ (盧龍軍節度使).
Wáng Zàn (王瓚) of Liáng (梁) attacked the southern city of Déshèng (德勝),
but did not conquer it.
In the tenth month,
the northern city of Déshèng (德勝) was expanded.
In the twelfth month,
the Liáng (梁) army was defeated north of the Hé (河) (Yellow River).
In the seventeenth year,
Zhū Yǒuqīan (朱友謙) raided Tóngzhōu (同州).
Liáng (梁) dispatched Liú Kuài (劉●) to attack Yǒuqīan (友謙).
Lǐ Cúnshěn (李存審) defeated the Liáng (梁) army at Tóngzhōu (同州).
In the first month of the eighteenth year,
a monk named Chuánzhēn (傳真) from Wèizhōu (魏州) presented a Tang (唐) imperial seal of mandate.
Zhāng Wénlǐ (張文禮), a general of Zhào (趙), assassinated his lord Róng (鎔).
Wénlǐ (文禮) came to request a commission.
In the second month,
Wénlǐ (文禮) was appointed Zhènzhōu Bīngmǎ Liúhòu (鎮州兵馬留後).
In the third month,

Zhū Yǒuqīan (朱友謙), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Hézhōng (河中); Lǐ Sìzhāo (李嗣昭), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Zhāoyì Jūn (昭義軍); Lǐ Cúnshěn (李存審), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Hénghǎi Jūn (橫海軍); Wáng Chǔzhí (王處直), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Yìwǔ Jūn (義武軍); Lǐ Sìyuán (李嗣源), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Ānguó Jūn (安國軍); Zhāng Wénlǐ (張文禮), Zhènzhōu Bīngmǎ Liúhòu (鎮州兵馬留後); Yán Bǎo (閻寶), concurrently Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Tiānpíng Jūn (天平軍); Lǐ Cúnzhāng (李存璋), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Dàtóng Jūn (大同軍); Lǐ Cúnjìn (李存進), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Zhènwǔ Jūn (振武軍); and Zhū Lìngdé (朱令德), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Kuāngguó Jūn (匡國軍),
requested the Wáng (王) to ascend the imperial throne.
The Wáng (王) declined thrice.
Yǒuqīan (友謙) and others requested thrice more.
The Wáng (王) said,
"I shall ponder this."
In the eighth month,
the Wáng (王) dispatched Fú Xí (符習), a former general of Wáng Róng (王鎔), the Wáng (王) of Zhào (趙), along with Yán Bǎo (閻寶) and Shǐ Jiàntáng (史建瑭), to attack Zhāng Wénlǐ (張文禮) at Zhènzhōu (鎮州).
Jiàntáng (建瑭) took Zhàozhōu (趙州).
Zhāng Wénlǐ (張文禮) died,
and his son Chǔjǐn (處瑾) closed the city gates and resisted.
In the ninth month,
Jiàntáng (建瑭) died in battle.
In the tenth month,
Dài Sīyuǎn (戴思遠) of Liáng (梁) attacked the northern city of Déshèng (德勝).
Lǐ Sìyuán (李嗣源) defeated him at Qīchéng (戚城).
Wáng Chǔzhí (王處直) rebelled and defected to the Qìdān (契丹).
His son Dū Yōu (都幽) held Chǔzhí (處直) captive and came to defect.
In the twelfth month,
the Qìdān (契丹) raided Zhuōzhōu (涿州),
and then Dìngzhōu (定州).
In the first month of the nineteenth year,
the Qìdān (契丹) were defeated at Xīnchéng (新城) and Wàngdū (望都).
The pursuit continued to Yōuzhōu (幽州).
In the third month,
Yán Bǎo (閻寶) was defeated at Zhènzhōu (鎮州),
and Lǐ Sìzhāo (李嗣昭) replaced him.
In the fourth month,
Sìzhāo (嗣昭) died in battle,
and Lǐ Cúnjìn (李存進) replaced him.
In the eighth month,
Liáng (梁) took Wèizhōu (衞州).
In the ninth month,
Cúnjìn (存進) defeated the Zhèn (鎮) people at Dōngyuán (東垣),
and Cúnjìn (存進) died in battle.
In the tenth month,
Lǐ Cúnshěn (李存審) captured Zhènzhōu (鎮州).
The Wáng (王) concurrently held the title of Chéngdé Jūn Jìedùshǐ (成德軍節度使).
In the spring, third month of Tóngguāng (同光) first year,
Lǐ Jìtāo (李繼韜) rebelled with Lùzhōu (潞州) and defected to Liáng (梁).
In summer, fourth month, on the Jǐsì (己巳) day,
the Emperor ascended the throne.
A general amnesty was declared,
the era name was changed,
and the dynastic name was Táng (唐).
Dòu Lúgé (豆盧革), Left Prime Minister of the Xíngtái (行臺), became Ménxià Shìláng (門下侍郎).
Lú Chéng (盧程), Right Prime Minister, became Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎), both holding the concurrent title of Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì (同中書門下平章事).
Guō Chóngtāo (郭崇韜), Zhōngmén Shǐ (中門使), and Zhāng Jūhàn (張居翰), Jiānjūn (監軍) of Zhāoyì (昭義), became Shūmì Shǐ (樞密使).
Wèizhōu (魏州) was designated as Dōngjīng (東京),
Tàiyuán (太原) as Xījīng (西京),
and Zhènzhōu (鎮州) as Běidū (北都).
The Shūmì Shǐ (樞密使)
in the former Táng (唐) was held by eunuchs.
Its position was very minor.
It was from this time that scholars were first included
and their power and authority became equal to that of the Zǎixiàng (宰相).
Therefore, they are recorded together with the Zǎixiàng (宰相).
In the intercalary month,
the imperial ancestors were posthumously honored as Huángdì (皇帝) and
their consorts as Huánghòu (皇后): Great-grandfather Zhíyí (執宜) and great-grandmother Cuī Shì (崔氏) were both given the posthumous title Zhāoliè (昭烈),
with the temple name Yìzǔ (懿祖).
Grandfather Guóchāng (國昌) and grandmother Qín Shì (秦氏) were both given the posthumous title Wénjǐng (文景),
with the temple name Xiànzǔ (獻祖).
Father was given the posthumous title Wǔ (武),
with the temple name Tàizǔ (太祖).
Temples were established in Tàiyuán (太原),
with seven temples from Táng Gāozǔ (唐高祖), Tàizōng (太宗), Yìzōng (懿宗), and Zhāozōng (昭宗) downwards.
On the Rén Yín (壬寅) day,
Lǐ Sìyuán (李嗣源) took Yùnzhōu (鄆州).
As the imperial ancestors were posthumously honored,
it is implied that temples were established for them.
Therefore, the word
"temple" is not written in most cases.
Here it is written
because four temples from Gāozǔ (高祖) downwards were established.
This is a major event,
but the old histories lost the date.
Later, Táng Tàizǔ (後唐太祖) established a large number of adopted sons' armies, such as Lǐ Sìzhāo (李嗣昭) and others.
Initially, all were given surnames and given names,
but they were not fully treated as sons.
Therefore, Lǐ Sìyuán (李嗣源) is written as such,
recording the surname and given name he was bestowed,
not as a son.
This is different from Yǒuwén (友文) and Cóngkē (從珂).
On the fifth month, Xīnyǒu (辛酉) day,
the Liáng (梁) people took the southern city of Déshèng (德勝).
In the sixth month,
they battled Wáng Yànzhāng (王彥章) at Xīnlěi (新壘),
defeating him.
In this month,
Lú Chéng (盧程) was dismissed.
I heard an elder tell me:
“Míngzōng, although of barbarian origin,
was pure and simple in character,
magnanimous and kind to people.”
Among the rulers of the Five Dynasties,
he is worthy of praise.
He once burned incense at night,
looked up to Heaven and prayed, saying:
“I am but a barbarian,
how am I fit to govern the world!
The world has been in chaos for a long time,
I pray that Heaven will soon give birth to a sage.”
From the beginning of his reign,
he reduced and dismissed palace women and musicians;
he abolished the imperial treasury,
and all tribute from the four quarters
was handed over to the relevant authorities.
When Guǎngshòu Diàn suffered a fire,
the authorities dealt with it,
and requested to add paint and vermilion.
He sighed profoundly and said:
“Heaven uses fire to warn me,
how can I increase extravagance and debauchery!”
One year it was drought,
and then it snowed.
He sat exposed in the courtyard,
and ordered the Wǔdé Sī that no snow should be swept in the palace,
saying:
“This is what Heaven has bestowed upon me.”
He frequently asked Prime Minister Féng Dào and others about the people's hardships.
When Dào and others said that grain and silk were cheap,
and the people suffered no epidemics,
he rejoiced and said:
“How can I bear this,
I should do good deeds with you,
to repay Heaven above.”
If an official committed embezzlement,
he would immediately put him to death,
saying:
“These are the pests of the people!”
He issued an imperial edict to commend honest officials like Sūn Yuè,
to serve as an example for the world.
His love for people and care for all creatures
indeed showed his intention to govern well.
When he ascended the throne,
he was already advanced in years,
not indulging in music and women,
nor enjoying hunting.
He reigned for seven years,

“For those who govern a nation, there are five things not to fear,
and six things to greatly fear: The misalignment of the three luminaries is not to be feared;
the manifestation of celestial anomalies is not to be feared;
the misleading rumors of petty people are not to be feared;
mountain collapses and rivers drying up are not to be feared;
droughts, floods, insects, and locusts are not to be feared;
but the hiding of worthy scholars is deeply to be feared;
the change of occupation of the four classes of people is deeply to be feared;
collusion between superiors and subordinates is deeply to be feared;
the decline of integrity and shame is deeply to be feared;
the confusion of true and false by praise and blame is deeply to be feared;

Those with insight all praised Chéng's words as sharply hitting the ailments of the time.

for all who govern a nation,

He followed in the campaign against Wáng Xiānzhī (王仙芝),

remaining in the capital.
The Lǐ (李) clan, since the time of Xiànzōng (憲宗), returned to Táng (唐) with their tribe.

sending Wáng Chǔcún (王處存) with troops to besiege Qīnrén Fāng (親仁坊),

Kèlìang (克讓), with his servants Hé Xiāngwēn (何相溫) and Shí Dìlì (石的歷) and more than ten cavalrymen,
drew their bows and spurred their horses,
breaking out of the siege.

Kèlìang (克讓) and his men shot and killed over a hundred men,

Kèlìang (克讓) fled to Yànmén (鴈門).
The next year,
Tàizǔ (太祖) again submitted to Táng (唐),
and Kèlìang (克讓) returned to guard the capital.
When Huáng Cháo (黃巢) attacked Cháng'ān (長安),
Kèlìang (克讓) defended Tóngguān (潼關).
He was defeated by the rebels
and fled to Nánshān (南山),
hiding in a Buddhist temple.

Kèxiū (克脩)
Kèxiū (克脩), courtesy name Chóngyuǎn (崇遠),
followed in the campaign against Páng Xùn (龐勛),
and for his merits, was appointed Governor (Cìshǐ, 刺史) of Shuòzhōu (朔州).

he appointed Kèxiū (克脩) as Fèngchéng (奉誠) Army Commander.

campaigned against Huáng Cháo (黃巢),
served as vanguard,
and was promoted to Commander of the Left Camp.

and appointed Kèxiū (克脩) as Jiedushi (節度使) of the Zhāoyì (昭義) Army.
He repeatedly went out to the east of the mountains to attack Fānglì (方立),
and also, with Lǐ Hǎnzhī (李罕之), attacked and plundered between Huái (懷) and Mèng (孟).
Afterwards,
Tàizǔ (太祖) personally led an attack on Fānglì (方立).
On his return journey, passing through Lù (潞),
Kèxiū (克脩) was by nature frugal and stingy,
and his provisions were very meager.
Tàizǔ (太祖) was greatly angered,
cursed and flogged him.
Kèxiū (克脩), shamed and indignant,
fell ill and died.
He had two sons: Sìbì (嗣弼) and Sìgōng (嗣肱).
Sìbì (嗣弼) was Governor of Zhuōzhōu (涿州).
In the 19th year of Tiānyòu (天祐)
the Qìdān (契丹) attacked and broke through Zhuōzhōu (涿州),
and Sìbì (嗣弼) died at the hands of the barbarians.
Sìgōng (嗣肱)
was brave and resourceful from a young age.
He followed Zhōu Déwēi (周德威) and repeatedly achieved military success,
becoming the Supreme Commander of Infantry and Cavalry.
When Lǐ Cúnshěn (李存審) defeated the Liáng (梁) army at Húbì (胡壁),
Sìgōng (嗣肱) captured one Liáng (梁) general.
When Liáng Tàizǔ (梁太祖) besieged Tiáoxiàn (蓨縣),
Sìgōng (嗣肱) followed Cúnshěn (存審) to relieve Tiáo (蓨).
The Liáng (梁) army withdrew,
and Sìgōng's (嗣肱) contribution was significant.
He was promoted exceptionally to Governor of Wèizhōu (蔚州) and Commander of All Infantry and Cavalry North of Yànmén (鴈門).
He was successively promoted to Governor of Zé (澤) and Dài (代) prefectures.
When Wáng Yù (王郁) of Xīnzhōu (新州) rebelled against Jìn (晉)
and fled to the Qìdān (契丹),
all the prefectures north of the mountains rebelled.
Sìgōng (嗣肱) retook Guī (媯), Rú (儒), and Wǔ (武) prefectures,
and was appointed Governor of Xīnzhōu (新州) and Commander of All Militias North of the Mountains.
In the spring of the first year of Tóngguāng (同光),
he died in office.
Kègōng (克恭)
Kègōng (克恭)
was initially the Commander of the Juéshèng (決勝) Army.
When Kèxiū (克脩) died,
Kègōng (克恭) was appointed in his place as Jiedushi (節度使) of the Zhāoyì (昭義) Army.
Kèxiū (克脩) was simple and frugal in character,
and the people of Lù (潞) had always been content with his governance,
and moreover, pitied his death by flogging.
Kègōng (克恭) was violent and unlawful,
and also inexperienced in military affairs.
Because of this, the people of Lù (潞) all resented him.
Kègōng (克恭) selected five hundred elite soldiers from his rear quarters
and presented them to Tàizǔ (太祖).
When they reached Tóngdī (銅鞮),
their general Féng Bà (馮霸) rebelled with his followers.
Tàizǔ (太祖) sent Lǐ Yuánshěn (李元審) to suppress them.
They fought at Qìnshuǐ (沁水),
where Yuánshěn (元審) was greatly defeated and wounded,
fleeing into Lùzhōu (潞州).
The deputy general Ān Jūshòu (安居受) also rebelled,
killing Kègōng (克恭) and Yuánshěn (元審).
He sent someone to summon Bà (霸),
but Bà (霸) refused the order.
Jūshòu (居受) became frightened and fled.
When he reached Chángzǐ (長子),
he was killed by commoners,
and his head was sent to Bà (霸).
Bà (霸) then entered Lùzhōu (潞州),
declared himself Acting Jiedushi (Liúhòu, 留後),
and allied himself with Liáng (梁).
Kèníng (克寧)
Kèníng (克寧)
was benevolent and filial,
the most virtuous among all his brothers.
He served Tàizǔ (太祖) with caution and diligence.
When Tàizǔ (太祖) fought against Hèlián Duó (赫連鐸) and Lǐ Kějǔ (李可舉) between Yún (雲) and Wèi (蔚),
later fled to Dádá (達靼),
and entered to defeat Huáng Cháo (黃巢),
Kèníng (克寧) never failed to accompany him.
When Tàizǔ (太祖) was stationed in Tàiyuán (太原),
he appointed Kèníng (克寧) as Grand Commander of all Barbarian and Han Troops for Internal and External Administration,
acting Grand Tutor (Tàibǎo, 太保) and Jiedushi (節度使) of the Zhènwǔ (振武) Army.
All matters of the army,
great or small, were decided by Kèníng (克寧).
When Tàizǔ (太祖) fell ill,
he summoned Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) to his side,
and entrusted him to Zhāng Chéngyè (張承業) and Kèníng (克寧), saying:
"I entrust the second son to you all."
When Tàizǔ (太祖) passed away,
Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) said to Kèníng (克寧):
"I am young and inexperienced,
and not yet familiar with general administration.
Although there is the late king's command,
I fear it is insufficient to handle important matters.
Uncle's merits and virtues are both high,
and the late king once entrusted you with administration.
I dare to burden my youngest uncle with the military and government affairs,
awaiting my establishment."
Kèníng (克寧) said:
"My elder brother's command
entrusted his son to me.
Who would dare to change it!"
He then bowed down facing north and made two prostrations to offer congratulations.
Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) then ascended the throne as King of Jìn (晉).
Initially,
when Tàizǔ (太祖) rose in the region between Yún (雲) and Shuò (朔),
many of the brave and fierce men he acquired
were adopted as sons.
And in his wars against heroes,
he ultimately achieved his hegemonic enterprise.
The adopted sons' contributions were numerous,
so he particularly favored and loved them.
Their clothing and ritual ranks were like those of嫡 (dí) legitimate sons.
The adopted sons each had elite soldiers under their command.
Relying on their merits, they acted wantonly,
and had often been shown leniency even in the late king's time.
When the new king ascended,
being young,
some feigned illness and did not attend court,
or appeared but did not bow.
The adopted sons Cún Hào (存顥) and Cún Shí (存實) told Kèníng (克寧):
"When an elder brother dies, a younger brother succeeds him;
this is the ancient way.
How can it be right for an uncle to bow to a nephew?
One's wealth and status in life
should be seized for oneself."
Kèníng (克寧) said:
"In our family for three generations,
fathers have been kind and sons filial.
If the late king's territory
has a rightful heir,
what more do I seek!"
Cài Wáng Xìn
was Gāo Zǔ's paternal cousin.
When Gāo Zǔ garrisoned Tàiyuán,
he appointed Xìn as Commander-in-Chief of the Xīngjié Army and Military Governor of Yìchéng Command,
then transferred him to command Xǔzhōu.
When Gāo Zǔ fell ill,
and Yǐn Dì was to be established as heir,
Yáng Bīn and others, who had received the dying command,
did not want Xìn to be in the capital.
So they sent Xìn to his post.
Xìn wept and departed.
Wherever Xìn went, he was greedy for bribes
and fond of killing.
When a soldier committed an offense,
Xìn would summon his wife and children,
and in front of them, he would disembowel, carve, and dismember the offender,
forcing them to eat his flesh.
Blood would flow abundantly before him,
while Xìn would command music and drink wine as if nothing was amiss.
When Yáng Bīn and the others died,
Xìn was greatly pleased.
He said to his subordinates:
"I once thought that Heaven had no eyes,
and it has kept me here in melancholy for three years!
The emperor is isolated
and almost fell into the hands of bandits.
Gentlemen, you may encourage me with a cup!"
After a while, hearing that troubles had broken out,
Xìn was too worried to eat.
When Zhōu Tài Zǔ's army mutinied at Chánzhōu,
Wáng Jùn sent former Shēnzhōu Prefect Mǎ Duó with troops to patrol and inspect Xǔzhōu.
Xìn then committed suicide.
When Zhōu Tài Zǔ ascended the throne,
he posthumously enfeoffed him as Cài Wáng.
The biography
places Yūn before Xìn;
this is merely for convenience in narrating events.
Zhōu Tài Zǔ's Family Biographies, Seventh, Empress Chái
Tài Zǔ had one empress and three consorts.
Empress Shèngmù Chái Shì
was from Yáoshān, Xíngzhōu.
She was from the same village as Tài Zǔ,
and thus returned to him.
When Tài Zǔ was humble,
he was fond of drinking, gambling, and acting as a knight-errant,
disregarding minor conduct.
The empress often advised him to stop.
Tài Zǔ's appearance was extraordinary and magnificent,
and the empress inwardly knew he was a distinguished person.
She served him with great prudence.
By the time Tài Zǔ ascended the throne,
the empress had already passed away.
So he issued an edict:
"The late Lady Chái Shì
is posthumously honored as empress,
with the posthumous title Shèngmù."
Consort Shū Yáng Shì
Consort Shū Yáng Shì
was from Zhēndìng, Zhènzhōu.
Her father, Hóngyù,
was the Junior Administrator of Zhēndìng.
As a child, the consort was chosen for her beauty and entered the palace of Zhào Wáng,
serving Wáng Róng.
When Róng was killed by Zhāng Wénlǐ,
Zhènzhōu was in chaos,
and the consort also became a refugee among the common people.
Later, she married Shí Guāngfǔ, a villager.
After several years,
Guāngfǔ died.
When Tài Zǔ's Lady Chái died,
he heard that the consort was beautiful and virtuous,
so he married her as his second wife.
Tài Zǔ was serving Hàn Gāo Zǔ in Tàiyuán at the time.
The consort died during the Tiānfú reign
and was buried in the near suburbs of Tàiyuán.
When Tài Zǔ ascended the throne,
in the ninth month of the first year of Guǎngshùn,
she was posthumously honored as Consort Shū.
He appointed the consort's younger brother, Tíngzhāng, as Right Fēilóng Envoy.
Tíngzhāng declined, saying:
"My father is old,
I wish to bestow it upon him."
Tài Zǔ said:
"I am thinking about it,
how could I forget your father!"
He immediately summoned Hóngyù.
Hóngyù was too old to travel,
so he was appointed Grand Master of Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon and Junior Administrator of Zhēndìng at his home.
When Tài Zǔ died,
he was buried in Sōnglíng.
The one empress and three consorts were all to be interred with him,
but Tàiyuán had not yet been conquered.
Shì Zōng ordered the officials to construct an empty tomb next to Sōnglíng to await them.
In the first year of Xiǎndé,
after Shì Zōng defeated Liú Mín at Gāopíng,
he then attacked Tàiyuán.
Tàiyuán closed its gates and was besieged,
so the consort's remains were moved and buried.
Consort Guì Zhāng Shì
Consort Guì Zhāng Shì
was from Zhēndìng, Zhènzhōu.
Her grandfather, Jì,
was the Judicial Commissioner of Chéngdé Army and Provisional Minister of War.
Her father, Tóngzhī,
served Zhào Wáng Wáng Róng as Counselor,
reaching the rank of Provisional Minister of Works.
When Róng died,
Zhènzhōu was in chaos.
Zhuāng Zōng sent Fú Cúnshěn of Yōuzhōu with troops to suppress Zhāng Wénlǐ.
His subordinate general, Wǔ Cóngjiàn, stayed at the consort's home
and saw that the consort was still young.
He pitied her,
and since Cóngjiàn's family was in Tàiyuán,
he took the consort back with him
to be his son's wife.
After a long time,
Tài Zǔ served Hàn Gāo Zǔ in Tàiyuán,
Lady Yáng died,
and Wǔ's son also died.
So he took the consort as his second wife.
When Tài Zǔ became noble,
she was repeatedly enfeoffed as Lady of Wú.
When Tài Zǔ entered the capital with his army,
Hàn sent Liú Zhū to slaughter his family,
and the consort and all her sons died.
When Tài Zǔ ascended the throne,
she was posthumously honored as Consort Guì.
Consort Dé Dǒng Shì (Sons Dǒng, Xìn; Nephews Shǒuyuàn, Fèngchāo, Xùn)
Consort Dé Dǒng Shì
was from Língshòu, Zhènzhōu.
Her grandfather, Wénguǎng,
was the Registrar of Shēnzhōu in the Táng dynasty.
Her father, Guāngsì,
was the Commandant of Zhāoqìng in Zhàozhōu.
As a child, the consort was intelligent and discerning.
As soon as she could speak,
she knew the musical scales upon hearing music.
At the age of seven,
Zhènzhōu was in chaos,
and her family lost her.
She was found by a staff officer from Lùzhōu,
who placed her in a basket and took her home.
The Lùzhou officer's wife had previously given birth to daughters
who did not survive.
She pitied the consort when she found her,
raised her as her own child,
loving her more than her biological children.
After five or six years,
the consort's family grieved and longed for her.
Her brother, Yǔ, searched for her among the people,
but no one knew her whereabouts.
The Lùzhōu officer served in the capital,
met Yǔ,
and happily returned her to him when she was thirteen years old.
Yǔ married her to Liú Jìnchāo, a villager.
Jìnchāo also served Jìn in an internal office.
When the Qìdān attacked the capital,
Jìnchāo died among the captives.
The consort lived as a widow in Luòyáng.
When Hàn Gāo Zǔ entered the capital from Tàiyuán,
Tài Zǔ followed.
Passing through Luòyáng,
he heard that the consort had virtuous conduct
and married her.
When Tài Zǔ established his state,
the central palace position was vacant,
so he appointed her as Consort Dé.
She died in the third year of Guǎngshùn
at the age of thirty-nine.
The consort had three elder brothers:
Yǔ reached the rank of Right Zànshàn Dàfū of the Crown Prince;
Xuánzhī and Zìmíng both reached the rank of Prefect.
Previously,
when the Emperor raised troops in Wèi,
Hàn sent troops to besiege the Emperor's residence.
At that time, Consort Guì Zhāng Shì and her sons Qīnggē, Yìgē,
and nephews Shǒuyún, Fèngchāo, Dìnggē
were all executed.
The mothers of Qīnggē and Yìgē
are unknown.
When Tài Zǔ ascended the throne,
he decreed that his second son, Qīnggē, be posthumously appointed Grand Tutor
and granted the name Dǒng;
his third son, Yìgē, be posthumously appointed Minister of Works
and granted the name Xìn;
his imperial nephew, Shǒuyún, be posthumously appointed General of the Left Leader of the Army Guard.
As the sound "Yún" was close to "Róng,"
to avoid Shì Zōng's taboo,
his name was changed to Shǒuyuàn;
Fèngchāo was posthumously appointed General of the Left Jìanmén Guard;
Dìnggē was posthumously appointed General of the Left Qiānniú Guard
and granted the name Xùn.
In the fourth year of Xiǎndé of Shìzōng, in the summer, fourth month, on the day Kuǐwèi,
an edict stated:
“Ritual arises from emotion,
and grace from grieving for the departed.
How much more so for those in the ranks of brothers,
upon whom profound sorrow falls.
Thus, the imperial younger brother, the posthumously granted Tàibǎo, Tóng
and the posthumously granted Sīkōng, Xìn,
whose grand fortunes were just beginning,
did not attain a great age.
This leaves me forever desolate,
and truly troubles my heart.
Tóng is to be posthumously granted Tàifù
and posthumously enfeoffed as Tán Wáng;
Xìn as Sītú
and Suī Wáng.”
Another edict stated:

“The imperial cousins, the posthumously granted Zuǒ Lǐngjūn Wèi Jiāngjūn, Shǒuyuàn; the posthumously granted Zuǒ Jiānmén Wèi Jiāngjūn, Fèngchāo; and the posthumously granted Zuǒ Qiānnú Wèi Jiāngjūn, Xùn, and others,
owing to the recent degenerate age,
did not enjoy a long life.
Whenever I think of their innocent deaths,
it is hard to forget my grief.
Shǒuyuàn is to be posthumously granted Zuǒ Wèi Dàjiāngjūn;
Fèngchāo, Yòu Wèi Dàjiāngjūn;
and Xùn, Yòu Wǔwèi Dàjiāngjūn.”

Empress Liú

Empress Fú
Empress Xuānyì Fú,

her father was Wèi Wáng Yànqīng.

his city was breached.
Chóngxùn knew he could not escape,
so he personally killed his family members with his own hands,
then proceeded to the empress.
The empress ran and hid,
concealing herself with curtains.
Chóngxùn, in a panic, could not find the empress,
and so committed suicide.
When the Hàn soldiers entered his house,
the empress sat calmly in the main hall,
and looking at the soldiers, said:
“Duke Guō and my father were old acquaintances,
you should not harm me!”
Seeing her, the soldiers dared not approach.
Tàizǔ heard of this
and thought it remarkable that a single woman could prevent unruly soldiers from harming her.
He marvelled at her,
and offered her comfort and encouragement,
then sent her back to Yànqīng.
The empress, grateful to Tàizǔ for not killing her,
bowed to Tàizǔ as her father.
Her mother, seeing that her daughter’s husband’s family had been exterminated,
but she alone had escaped death by the sword,
considered it a heavenly blessing
and wanted her to shave her head and become a nun.
The empress refused, saying:
“Life and death are fated;
it is Heaven’s will.
Why must I wantonly disfigure my hair and body?!”
Tàizǔ had shown kindness to the empress,
and Shìzōng was particularly sharp and astute by nature.
When he heard of the empress’s character,
he admired her even more.
After Lady Liú died,
he then took her as his second wife.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
she was enthroned as empress.
Shìzōng was impetuous and prone to violent outbursts.
However, he often regretted his anger afterwards.
Whenever he was angry with his attendants,
the empress would always calmly observe his mood,
and gradually intercede for them,
and Shìzōng’s anger would also subside.
Because of this, he respected her even more.
When Shìzōng campaigned in Huái,
the empress advised him strongly against going in person,
but Shìzōng did not listen.
The campaign dragged on without success,
and they encountered intense heat and rain.
The empress fell ill from worry and passed away.
Discussions arose, given that troops were still deployed,
to reduce the mourning rites.
Consequently, all officials mourned at the West Palace,
and shed their mourning clothes after three days.
The emperor also shed his after seven days,
and she was buried in Xīnzhèng,
her mausoleum named Yìlíng.
When Mòdì ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì,
and transferred to govern Tiānpíng.
When Jiǎng Yīn rebelled in Xúzhōu,
Cúnjié was sent to attack and defeat him.
For this achievement, he was promoted to Tàiwèi.
As Liáng and Jìn confronted each other on the river,
Cúnjié fell ill with dysentery.
While Liáng and Jìn were locked in bitter struggle,
Cúnjié's loyalty and indignation were greatly roused.
He managed the army and supervised his officers,
never once mentioning his illness.
When his illness became critical,
he was summoned back to the capital.
Before he died,
he said to his son Zhīyè:
"Loyalty and filial piety
are what my son should embody."
He did not speak of anything else.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàishī.
Zhāng Guībà (younger brothers Guīhòu, Guībiàn)
Zhāng Guībà
was a native of Qīnghé.
Mòdì married his daughter,
who became Dèfēi.
Guībà, when young, and his younger brothers Guīhòu and Guībiàn all followed Huáng Cháo.
When Cháo was defeated and fled east,
the Guībà brothers surrendered to Liáng.
When Qín Zōngquán attacked Biàn,
Guībà distinguished himself in several battles.
Zhāng Zhì's army was stationed at Chìgāng.
When Zhì challenged with cavalry,
an arrow struck Guībà.
Guībà pulled it out
and shot it back at the enemy.
With one shot, he killed him,
seized his horse, and returned.
Tàizǔ, observing from Gāoqiu,
was greatly impressed,
rewarding him with gold and silk,
and also giving him the horse.
He sent Guībà with five hundred archers to lie in ambush in Huáng,
while Tàizǔ led several hundred cavalry as skirmishers.
Passing Zhì's palisade,
Zhì's troops came out to pursue Tàizǔ.
Guībà sprang his ambush,
killing a thousand of Zhì's soldiers
and capturing dozens of horses.
When Tàizǔ attacked Càizhōu,
Cài general Xiāo Hào fiercely attacked Tàizǔ's camp.
Guībà, without waiting to ask permission,
divided his forces with Xú Huáiyù and sallied out from the southeast wall gate.
They jointly attacked and defeated them,
allowing Tàizǔ to withdraw his camp.
Tàizǔ attacked Yǎn and Yùn,
and captured Cáozhōu.
He ordered Guībà to guard it with several thousand troops.
They fought against Zhū Jǐn at Jīnxiāng,
and thoroughly defeated him.
He also broke Púzhōu.
When the Jìn people attacked Wèi,
Guībà followed Gé Cóngzhōu to relieve Wèi.
Fighting at Huánshuǐ,
Guībà captured Kèyòng's son Luòluò and handed him over to the Wèi people.
He also defeated Liú Rén'gōng at Nèihuáng,
his achievements surpassing those of all other generals.
In the second year of Guānghuà (904 CE),
he temporarily governed Xíngzhōu.
He was transferred to be the Prefect of Láizhōu,
and appointed Zuǒwèi Shàngjiāngjūn and Cáozhōu Cìshǐ.
In the first year of Kāipíng (907 CE),
he was appointed Yòu Lónghǔ Tǒngjūn and Zuǒ Xiāowèi Shàngjiāngjūn.
In the second year (908 CE),
he was appointed Héyáng Jiédùshǐ,
and died of illness.
His son, Hànjié,
served Mòdì as a high official,
and held power due to Zhāng Dèfēi.
When Liáng fell,
Táng Zhuāngzōng entered Biàn,
and Hànjié's entire clan was executed.
His younger brother Guīhòu,
courtesy name Dékūn.
As a general, he was skilled with bow and spear,
and capable of defeating many with few.
When Zhāng Zhì was stationed at Chìgāng,
Guīhòu fought Zhì alone in front of the formation.
Zhì, exhausted, retreated,
and the other generals pressed the attack.
Zhì was then utterly defeated.
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased
and appointed him Qíjǐng.
When Liáng attacked Shí Pǔ,
Guīhòu led his subordinates to advance first to Jiǔlǐshān.
They encountered Xú soldiers and fought.
The former Liáng general Chén Fán had rebelled and was in Xú.
Guīhòu recognized him upon sight,
glared and cursed loudly,
then galloped directly towards him to capture him.
An arrow struck his left eye.
When Chēn Wáng Yǒuyù attacked Yùn
and was stationed in Púzhōu,
Tàizǔ arrived later.
Yǒuyù moved his palisade,
and Tàizǔ lost track of him.
Tàizǔ eventually encountered Yùn's troops.
Tàizǔ ascended a high point to observe.
The Yùn troops numbered only about a thousand.
Tàizǔ and Guīhòu, with the Tīngzǐ Army, charged directly at them.
As the battle joined,
a large force of Yùn troops arrived.
Guīhòu judged they could not hold,
and with several dozen cavalry, escorted Tàizǔ back first.
Guīhòu's horse was struck by an arrow and collapsed,
so he fought on foot with his spear.
Tàizǔ returned to the army camp
and sent Zhāng Jūn to gallop back to rescue him,
believing he was surely dead.
Guīhòu had been struck by more than ten arrows.
He returned on Jūn's horse.
When Tàizǔ saw him,
he wept and said:
"With you alive,
what is the loss of an army to count?"
He ordered him to be carried back to Xuānwǔ.
He was promoted to Yòu Shénwǔ Tǒngjūn,
and successively served as Prefect of Míng, Jìn, and Jiàng prefectures.
He fought repeatedly against the Jìn people and never yielded.
In the first year of Gānhuà (911 CE),
he was appointed Zhènguó Jūn Jiédùshǐ,
and died of illness.
His son was Hànqīng.
Guībiàn,
as a general, was also skilled in battle.
In the early Kāipíng era, he was Huázhōu Chángjiàn Zhǐhuīshǐ.
His son was Hànróng.
When Liáng fell,
they were all executed with their clans.
Wáng Chóngshī
Wáng Chóngshī
was a native of Chángshè, Xǔzhōu.
He was a taciturn man, full of wisdom,
and skilled with sword and spear.
When Qín Zōngquán captured Xǔzhōu,
Chóngshī escaped and returned to Liáng.
He followed Tàizǔ to pacify Cài,
and attacked Yǎn and Yùn,
serving as Bášān Jūn Zhǐhuīshǐ.
Chóngshī fought bitterly between Qí and Lǔ,
and his might shook his enemies.
He was promoted to Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Tàizǔ attacked Púzhōu.
After it was breached,
the people of Pú piled up straw and set it on fire,
preventing the Liáng army from entering.
At this time,
Chóngshī was suffering from a metal-wound,
lying in his tent.
When the generals urged him,
Chóngshī immediately rose,
took all the felt blankets in the army, soaked them with water,
and covered the fire with them.
He led elite soldiers with short weapons to storm in.
The Liáng army followed them all in,
and thus Púzhōu was captured.
Chóngshī sustained eight or nine wounds,
and his soldiers carried him back.
When Tàizǔ heard of it,
he exclaimed in surprise:
"How can I gain Púzhōu and lose Chóngshī!"
He had doctors treat him,
and he recovered after more than a month.
When Wáng Shīfàn surrendered,
he presented Chóngshī as the Acting Administrator of Qīngzhōu.
He was successively promoted to Yòuguó Jūn Jiédùshǐ and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
He held this position for several years,
and had great prestige and benevolence.
Chóngshī had an old grudge with Liú Hàn.
Hàn often sowed discord about him with Tàizǔ,
and Tàizǔ became suspicious of him.
Chóngshī sent his general Zhāng Jūnliàn to attack Bīn and Fèng to the west without asking for permission first.
Jūnliàn's troops suffered a minor defeat.
Tàizǔ, because he had unilaterally launched troops
and thereby diminished the nation's prestige,
was about to summon and punish him.
He sent Liú Hàn to replace Chóngshī.
Chóngshī did not know Tàizǔ was angry with him.
When Hàn arrived,
Chóngshī did not go out to welcome him,
meeting him at the Green Gate.
His礼 (decorum/etiquette) was also arrogant.
Hàn then rushed to inform Tàizǔ,
claiming that Chóngshī had rebellious intentions.
Tàizǔ became even angrier.
He demoted Chóngshī to Xīzhōu Cìshǐ,
then again to Yázhōu Sīhù Cānjūn.
Before he could depart,
he was granted death.
Xú Huáiyù
Initially,
Yánlǎng and Gǎo jointly managed confidential matters.
Yánlǎng took sole charge of affairs.
Among the generals who were to receive a prefecture,
their merits and seniority were not prioritized.
Those who gave more bribes received good prefectures;
those who gave few or no bribes received bad prefectures,
or were delayed indefinitely.
Because of this, everyone resented him.
Gǎo was inwardly troubled by this,
but could not contend with him.
He merely ate his fill and rested high on his pillow every day.
Whenever Yánlǎng discussed matters,
he would hang his head and feign sleep, paying no attention.
When the Jìn troops entered,
Yánlǎng fled alone on horseback to Nánshān.
Passing his home,
he pointed and sighed, saying:
"I accumulated three hundred thousand *qián* here;
I wonder who will take it!"
He was then killed by the pursuing soldiers.
Jìn Gāozǔ heard that Gǎo had always avoided Yánlǎng's affairs,
and pitied him.
Later, he reinstated him as a general.
He died more than a year later.
Zhuānměi served Jìn as Dàlǐ Qīng [Grand Judge],
and died during the Kāiyùn reign.
When Jìn was about to rise,
the Deposed Emperor appointed Zhāoyìn as Zhōngshū Shìláng [Secretary of the Central Secretariat] and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì [Chancellor].
He was sent out as Háyáng Jiédù Shǐ [Military Governor of Háyáng].
He, Shěnqián, and Wényù, all met unknown ends.
Alas,
the principles of fortune and misfortune, success and failure,
how can one not be cautious!
Zhāng Méng's divine words proved true,
but how could he know that they would not lead to disaster!
What I have recorded
is largely like this.
Readers can ponder deeply.
When the Deposed Emperor rose,
those with whom he plotted and deliberated
were merely these five or six people.
Considering the principles of their rebellion and loyalty,
even if there were wise men to advise them,
they might not necessarily avoid defeat,
much less these five or six people!
Therefore, I have included this narrative and appended it to Yánlǎng's account,
to show the beginning and end of their situation.
Kāng Sīlì
Kāng Sīlì
was originally a native of various tribes in Shānyīn.
As a youth, he was a cavalry commander,
and followed Zhuāngzōng to defeat the Liáng forces at Jiāchéng,
and fought at Báixiāng.
He was repeatedly promoted for his merits to Túqí Zhǐhuīshǐ [Commander of Elite Cavalry].
After Míngzōng ascended the throne,
he successively served as Cǐshǐ [Prefect] of Yìng and Lán prefectures, Sùzhōu Tuánliàn Shǐ [Militia Commissioner of Sùzhōu], and Zhāowǔ Jūn Jiédù Shǐ [Military Governor of Zhāowǔ Army].
He was then moved to command Bǎoyì,
and in all these posts, he governed well.
When Lùwáng Cóngkē rebelled at Fèngxiáng,
Mǐndì dispatched Wáng Sītóng and others to suppress him.
Sīlì had a thousand five hundred soldiers of the Pěngshèng and Yǔlín divisions.
He then assigned a thousand Yǔlín soldiers to Sītóng.
When Sītóng reached Fèngxiáng,
his army mutinied
and surrendered to Cóngkē.
Upon hearing this, Sīlì
wanted to execute all the families of the thousand Yǔlín soldiers,
but before he could,
Cóngkē's troops had already arrived.
Sīlì then garrisoned the city with his Pěngshèng troops.
Cóngkē's troops pressed against the city,
shouting:
"Ten thousand Western soldiers are supporting the new emperor.
Can you five hundred men resist?
You will only doom the Shǎnxī people to death!"
Hearing this, the Pěngshèng soldiers
all laid down their armor.
Sīlì then opened the gates and welcomed Cóngkē.
When the Deposed Emperor ascended the throne,
he was quite displeased with Sīlì because he initially had no intention of surrendering.
He was moved to Ānyuǎn,
then to Ānguó,
and due to old age, was dismissed as Yòu Shénwǔ Tǒngjūn [Commander of the Right Divine Martial Army].
When Shí Jìngtáng rebelled at Tàiyuán,
the Deposed Emperor appointed Sīlì as Běimiàn Xíngyíng Mǎjūn Dūzhǐhuīshǐ [Commander-in-Chief of Cavalry for the Northern Campaign].
The Deposed Emperor went to Huáizhōu,
and sent Sīlì to lead the cavalry accompanying him to Tuanbó Gǔ to relieve Zhāng Jìngdá.
Before he arrived,
Jìngdá had died,
and Yáng Guāngyuǎn had surrendered to Jìn.
Sīlì fell ill
and died on the way.
When Jìn Gāozǔ entered and ascended the throne,
he posthumously granted him the title of Tàizǐ Shàoshī [Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince].
Kāng Yìchéng
Kāng Yìchéng,
courtesy name Xìnchén,
was a native of the Three Tribes north of Dài.
He served the Jìn king with his archery and horsemanship.
During Zhuāngzōng's time, he was Túqí Zhǐhuīshǐ [Commander of Elite Cavalry].
He followed Míngzōng to suppress Zhào Zàilǐ.
When they reached Wèi, the army mutinied.
Yìchéng stepped forward to enumerate Zhuāngzōng's mistakes,
and advised Míngzōng to head south.
After Míngzōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Pěngshèng Zhǐhuīshǐ [Commander of the Pěngshèng Division],
and concurrently served as Fénzhōu Cǐshǐ [Prefect of Fénzhōu].
He followed in the defeat of Zhū Shǒuyīn,
and was promoted to Shìwèi Qīnjūn Mǎbùjūn Dūzhǐhuīshǐ [Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Guards' Cavalry and Infantry],
concurrently serving as Háyáng Sānchéng Jiédù Shǐ [Military Governor of the Three Prefectures of Háyáng].
He was sent out as Shānnán Dōngdào Jiédù Shǐ [Military Governor of the Eastern Shānnán Circuit],
then returned to be Qīnjūn Dūzhǐhuīshǐ [Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Guards],
concurrently serving in Háyáng,
and was granted the title Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāng Shì [Chancellor].
Qínwáng Cóngróng was always arrogant.
He served as Hénán Yǐn [Prefect of Hénán],
commanded the Six Armies,
and was appointed Dà Yuánshuài [Grand Marshal].
All the Tang ministers feared disaster would strike them,
and sought to distance themselves.
Only Yìchéng was wholeheartedly devoted to him,
and sent his son to serve in Qínwáng's residence.
When Míngzōng fell ill,
Cóngróng planned to enter the palace with troops.
Tang ministers Zhū Hóngzhāo, Féng Yūn, and others all deemed it impermissible,
but Yìchéng alone played both sides.
Cóngróng had already raised troops
and reached Tiānjīn Qiáo.
Hóngzhāo and others entered
and reported his rebellion.
Míngzōng tearfully summoned Yìchéng
and ordered him to handle the situation himself,
but Yìchéng ultimately did not dispatch troops.
Mǎjūn Zhǐhuīshǐ [Cavalry Commander] Zhū Hóngshí attacked Cóngróng with his troops.
Cóngróng was defeated and fled,
and was killed.
Sānsī Shǐ [Commissioner of Finance] Sūn Yuè had once spoken to Féng Yūn about Cóngróng's inevitable defeat.
Yìchéng heard of this and was displeased.
When Cóngróng died,
Yìchéng then led his troops into Hénán Fǔ [Hénán Prefecture],
and summoned Yuè to inspect Cóngróng's family assets.
When Yuè arrived,
Yìchéng, amidst the chaos,
ordered men to shoot him.
Yuè fled to Tōnglì Fāng where he was killed.
Míngzōng could not investigate the matter.
After Yìchéng killed Yuè,
and also because of Cóngróng,
he had a rift with Hóngshí.
When Mǐndì ascended the throne, Hóngshí often prided himself on his achievement of executing Cóngróng, and Yìchéng grew even more resentful.
Xīfǔ's nature was narrow-minded and impetuous.
He once sent someone at night to knock on the palace gate to report a serious matter,
saying that Lǐ Jūn (李筠), the Yágūan (牙官) of the river weir, had reported the current army's intention to rebel.
The next morning,
an investigation revealed it to be groundless,
so Jūn was executed.
The soldiers went to Ān Chónghuì (安重誨) to demand Xīfǔ (希甫) be handed over to them.
At that time,
Míngzōng (明宗) was about to perform rituals at the Southern Suburb.
The day before the fasting,
all the officials practiced the ceremony in the palace hall.
The chancellors Féng Dào (馮道) and Zhào Fèng (趙鳳),
Qínwáng (秦王) Cóngróng (從榮), the Hénán Yǐn (河南尹),
and the Shūmìshǐ (樞密使) Ān Chónghuì (安重誨) awaited their turn outside the Yuèhuá Mén (月華門).
Xīfǔ (希甫) and the officials of the two departments entered first.
Dào (道) and the others sat under the corridor and did not rise.
After Xīfǔ (希甫) came out,
he summoned the Tángtóu Zhíshěng Cháotáng Qūshǐguān (堂頭直省朝堂驅使官)
and reprimanded them, asking why the chancellors and Shūmì (樞密) did not rise upon seeing the officials of the two departments.
He then launched into a great tirade.
That night,
he feigned illness and returned to his residence.
More than a month later,
for causing unrest among the troops with the false accusation against Lǐ Jūn (李筠),
he was demoted to Sīhù Cānjūn (司戶參軍) of Lánzhōu (嵐州),
and died at the place of his demotion.
Liú Zàn
Liú Zàn (劉贊)
was a native of Wèizhōu (魏州).
His father, Pín (玭), was a county magistrate.
When Zàn (贊) first began his studies,
he wore a blue cloth shirt and jacket.
Whenever they ate, Pín (玭) would eat meat himself,
but would serve Zàn (贊) vegetables separately at the foot of the bed,
telling him: "Meat
is the stipend of a gentleman.
If you desire it,
then study diligently to attain a stipend.
My meat
is not your food."
From then on, Zàn (贊) studied even harder
and passed the Jìnshì (進士) examination.
He became the Pànguān (判官) for Luó Shàowēi (羅紹威),
then left to become the Xúnguān (巡官) for Zūyōngshǐ (租庸使) Zhào Yán (趙巖),
and later the Yántiě Pànguān (鹽鐵判官) for Kǒng Qiān (孔謙).
During Míngzōng's (明宗) reign,
he was successively promoted to Zhōngshū Shèrén (中書舍人), Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞), and Xíngbù Shìláng (刑部侍郎).
He administered his office according to law,
and the powerful and influential could not bribe him for personal favors.
At that time,
Qínwáng (秦王) Cóngróng (從榮) held military power and was arrogant,
making many mistakes.
Those who spoke on affairs of state requested that a tutor be appointed to guide him.
The great ministers feared the king
and dared not decide the matter themselves,
so they asked the king to choose for himself.
Qínwáng (秦王) then requested Zàn (贊).
Zàn (贊) was consequently appointed Mìshū Jiān (祕書監)
and tutor to Qínwáng (秦王).
Zàn (贊) wept and said: "Calamity is about to befall us!"
Qínwáng (秦王) had requested over ten officials for his princely mansion,
most of whom were frivolous and treacherous individuals,
who daily offered flattery to inflate the king's ego.
Only Zàn (贊) calmly offered remonstrance,
always according to the correct path.
Qínwáng (秦王) once ordered his guests to compose essays in his presence.
Zàn (贊), considering himself a tutor,
was ashamed to be grouped with such petty individuals.
Although he reluctantly took up his brush,
he showed displeasure.
Qínwáng (秦王) disliked this.
Later, he instructed his attendants not to admit Zàn (贊) when he came.
Zàn (贊) also stopped going,
only visiting the mansion once a month.
After retiring, he would close his door and avoid all social contact.
Shortly thereafter, Qínwáng (秦王) indeed suffered defeat and died.
When the Táng (唐) ministers discussed which of the king's subordinate officials should be implicated,
Féng Dào (馮道) said: "Yuánshuài Pànguān (元帥判官) Rèn Zàn (任贊) and Qínwáng (秦王) were not previously close,
and he was in office for less than a month.
Zhànshì (詹事) Wáng Jūmǐn (王居敏) and Liú Zàn (劉贊) were both disliked by the king for their uprightness.
Hénánfǔ Pànguān (河南府判官) Sītú Xǔ (司徒詡) had been home on sick leave for a long time.
All of them should be deemed not privy to the conspiracy.
However, Zīyì Cānjūn (諮議參軍) Gāo Niǎn (高輦) was closest to the king.
Niǎn (輦) should legally be put to death;
the rest can be gradually pardoned or have their sentences reduced."
Zhū Hóngzhāo (朱弘昭) said: "You gentlemen do not understand his true intention.
If Qínwáng (秦王) had managed to enter the Guāngzhèng Mén (光政門),
how would he have treated Zàn (贊) and the others?
Would we still have our families?
Moreover, the law distinguishes between principals and accessories.
Now that Qínwáng (秦wáng), his wife, sons, and daughters are all dead,
Zàn (贊) and the others are fortunate to merely keep their lives!"
Dào (道) and the others found it difficult to argue.
And Féng Yūn (馮贇) also strongly argued against it.
Zàn (贊) and the others were then spared death.
Thereupon, Gāo Niǎn (高輦) was sentenced to death,
and Rèn Zàn (任贊) and seventeen others were all exiled for life.
At first,
when Zàn (贊) heard of Qínwáng's (秦王) defeat,
he immediately donned white clothes and rode a donkey, awaiting his fate.
Someone told Zàn (贊) that he would merely be dismissed from office.
Zàn (贊) said:
"How can the emperor's heir be slain
while his retainers merely lose their offices?
Not to die is already fortunate!"
Afterwards, Zàn (贊) was exiled to be a commoner in Lánzhōu (嵐州).
In the second year of Qīngtài (清泰),
an imperial edict ordered his return home.
He fell ill and died
at Shíhuì Guān (石會關) while en route.
Hé Zàn
Hé Zàn (何瓚)
was a native of Mǐn (閩).
At the end of the Táng (唐) dynasty, he passed the Jìnshì (進士) examination.
When Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) was Jìdùshǐ (節度使) of Tàiyuán (太原),
he was appointed Pànguān (判官).
Whenever Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) went on military campaigns,
he left Zhāng Chéngyè (張承業) to guard Tàiyuán (太原).
After Chéngyè (承業) died,
Zàn (瓚) took his place as acting Liúshǒushì (留守事).
Zàn (瓚) was bright and astute,
skilled in official matters.
He appeared outwardly relaxed and simple, but was inwardly quite thorough and meticulous.
When Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) established his grand title in Yèdū (鄴都),
Zàn (瓚) was appointed Jiàn Yì Dàfū (諫議大夫).
Zàn (瓚), fearing that Zhuāngzōng's (莊宗) endeavor would not succeed,
requested to remain as Liúshǒu (留守) of Běijīng (北京).
Zàn (瓚) had old ties with Míngzōng (明宗).
When Míngzōng (明宗) ascended the throne,
Zàn (瓚) was summoned back
and met in the inner palace.
Míngzōng (明宗) inquired about him for a long time,
and then appointed Zàn (瓚) as Xīchuān Jìdù Fùshǐ (西川節度副使).
At this time,
Mèng Zhīxiáng (孟知祥) already harbored ambitions.
He was treating his Fùshǐ (副使) Zhào Jìliáng (趙季良) as his confidant.
Hearing that Zàn (瓚) was to replace him,
he urgently memorialized to retain Jìliáng (季良).
Consequently, Zàn (瓚) was reassigned as Xíngjūn Sīmǎ (行軍司馬).
Zàn (瓚) was ashamed to decline the position himself,
so he went reluctantly,
with Míngzōng (明宗) giving him generous gifts.
Initially,
Zhīxiáng (知祥) was Mǎbùjūn Dōu Yúhóu (馬步軍都虞候) in Běijīng (北京),
while Zàn (瓚) was Liúshǒu (留守) of Tàiyuán (太原).
Zhīxiáng (知祥) treated Zàn (瓚) with military deference,
and Zàn (瓚) always kept him to the law.
Zhīxiáng (知祥) was initially displeased.
But when Zàn (瓚) became Sīmǎ (司馬),
Zhīxiáng (知祥) still grudgingly treated him very well.
When Zhīxiáng (知祥) rebelled,
he dismissed Zàn (瓚) from his Sīmǎ (司馬) post
and confined him to his private residence.
Zàn (瓚) died consumed by resentment.
Jiàokān Jì (校勘記)
Jìn Chén Zhuàn (晉臣傳) Volume 17 Sāng Wéihàn
Sāng Wéihàn (桑維翰), courtesy name Guóqiáo (國僑),
was a native of Hénán (河南).
He was ugly,
short in stature with a long face.
He often looked at himself in a mirror and remarked with self-admiration:
"A seven-foot body
is not as good as a one-foot face."
He harbored great ambitions of becoming a high-ranking official.
When he first sat for the Jìnshì (進士) examination,
the chief examiner disliked his surname,
because
"Sāng" (桑)
and "Sàng" (喪)
were homophones.
Someone advised him not to necessarily take the Jìnshì (進士) exam,
suggesting he could seek office through other means.
Wéihàn (維翰) responded with emotion,
then wrote the essay "Rì Chū Fúsāng Fù" (日出扶桑賦) to express his ambition.
He also cast an iron inkstone and showed it to people, saying:
"When this inkstone is worn out, then I will change my ambition and seek office otherwise."
Ultimately, he passed the Jìnshì (進士) examination.
Jìn Gāozǔ (晉高祖) appointed him Zhǎng Shūjì (掌書記) of Héyáng Jìdù (河陽節度),
and thereafter he always kept him by his side.
Zhōu Tàizǔ went out to govern Wèizhōu.
Shǐ Hóngzhào proposed taking the Bureau of Military Affairs position with him,
but Sū Féngjí and Yáng Bīn thought it was not permissible.
Shǐ Hóngzhào resented this.
The next day,
they met for a drink at Dòu Zhēnggù’s residence.
Shǐ Hóngzhào, raising his goblet with a stern voice, toasted Zhōu Tàizǔ, saying:
“Yesterday in the court discussion,
why was there disagreement?
Today I drink this with you.”
Féngjí and Bīn also raised large goblets, saying:
“This is a matter of the state,
why must you take it to heart!”
And they all drank their cups dry.
Shǐ Hóngzhào said:
“To bring peace to the court,
and settle chaos,
one simply needs long spears and great swords.
How can ‘hairy cones’
be of any use?”
The Three Department Commissioner, Wáng Zhāng, said:
“Without ‘hairy cones’,
how would the military tax be collected?”
“Hairy cones”
referred to writing brushes.
Shǐ Hóngzhào fell silent.
Another day,
they met for a drink at Wáng Zhāng’s residence.
When the wine was flowing freely,
they played a hand gesture game.
Shǐ Hóngzhào couldn’t play it.
Yán Jìnqīng, the Commissioner of the Guest Bureau, who sat next to Shǐ Hóngzhào,
repeatedly taught him.
Sū Féngjí joked:
“With someone named Yán sitting here,
why worry about a penalty drink!”
Shǐ Hóngzhào’s wife was named Yán,
and she was a singing girl from a tavern.
He took this as a jab at himself
and became furious,
cursing Féngjí with foul language.
Féngjí did not respond.
Shǐ Hóngzhào wanted to strike him,
but Féngjí left first.
Shǐ Hóngzhào rose, grabbing a sword, wanting to pursue him.
Yáng Bīn tearfully said:
“Sū Gōng
is a prime minister of Hàn.
If you kill him,
where would you place the Son of Heaven?”
Shǐ Hóngzhào galloped away on his horse,
and Bīn saw him to his residence and returned.
From then on, the generals and ministers were like fire and water.
Yǐndì sent Wáng Jùn to host a banquet at Gōngzǐ Tíng to reconcile them.
At this time,
Lǐ Yè, Guō Yǔnmíng, Hòu Zàn, Niè Wénjìn, and others were in power,
and disliked the executive officials.
As Yǐndì grew older,
he was controlled by his powerful ministers
and often expressed resentment.
Lǐ Yè and others seized the opportunity to slander them,
claiming that Shǐ Hóngzhào’s power intimidated the emperor,
and that if he were not eliminated, he would surely cause trouble.
Yǐndì greatly desired to eliminate them.
At night, he heard the sound of armor being forged in the workshops,
and thought that soldiers had arrived.
He did not sleep until dawn.
Because of this, he secretly conspired with Lǐ Yè and others within the palace.
On the thirteenth day of the tenth month of the third year of Qiányòu,
Shǐ Hóngzhào, Yáng Bīn, Wáng Zhāng, and others entered the court.
They sat in the east corridor of Guǎngzhèng Diàn.
Dozens of armed guards emerged from within the palace,
captured Shǐ Hóngzhào, Bīn, and Zhāng, and beheaded them,
and also exterminated their three clans.
After Shǐ Hóngzhào’s death,
the Emperor sat in Chóngyuán Diàn and summoned his officials,
informing them that Shǐ Hóngzhào and the others had plotted rebellion.
None of the officials could respond.
He then summoned the various military commanders to Wànsuì Diàn.
The Emperor said:
“Shǐ Hóngzhào and the others wielded exclusive power,
causing you all to constantly worry about violent death.
Today I can be your lord!”
All the military commanders bowed.
When Zhōu Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he posthumously enfeoffed Shǐ Hóngzhào as Prince Zhèng
and buried him with due rites.
Yáng Bīn
Yáng Bīn was
a native of Guànshì in Wèizhōu.
In his youth, he served as a record-keeping clerk in the prefecture.
When Kǒng Qiān, the Commissioner of Taxation, was in charge of the Department of State Finance,
he appointed Bīn as a supervising official.
He successively served as manager of the provisioning office in the three prefectures of Mèng, Huá, and Yùn.
He served Hàn Gāozǔ as the Right Capital Overseer.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed him Commissioner of Military Affairs.
Bīn came from a humble background as a minor official,
and disliked literati.
He and Sū Féngjí and others were in mutual contention within the court.
Féngjí prompted Lǐ Táo to submit a memorial to dismiss Bīn and Zhōu Tàizǔ from their positions as Commissioners of Military Affairs.
Bīn tearfully pleaded before Empress Dowager Lǐ.
The Empress Dowager was angered
and dismissed Lǐ Táo from his prime ministership,
and promoted Bīn to Grand Secretary of the Central Secretariat, concurrently Minister of Personnel, and Co-equal with the Grand Administrator.
At this time,
Féngjí and Yǔ Guī often appointed officials through private bribery,
making many errors.
When Bīn became prime minister,
all matters, large or small,
had to be presented to Bīn first.
Only if Bīn approved
would they be reported to the emperor.
He deeply reformed Féngjí’s practices.
All officials who gained office through family influence
or were appointed as clerks by various departments
were dismissed without exception.
Although Bīn was skilled in official affairs,
he lacked a grand vision.
He believed that for the state,
the granaries should be full,
and the army strong and complete,
and that ritual, music, and cultural artifacts were all empty formalities.
Thus, holding great political power, he focused on petty details.
For example, former officials were not allowed to reside outside the capital,
and all travelers in the realm
had to be issued travel permits before they could proceed.
Within a few days,
public sentiment was greatly disturbed,
and Bīn, realizing it was impractical, stopped.
Bīn often discussed matters with Wáng Zhāng before the Emperor.
The Emperor said:
“After the matter is put into practice,
do not allow anyone to speak ill of it!”
Bīn quickly said:
“Your Majesty need only silence your voice,
your humble servant is here.”
Those who heard it trembled.
Empress Dowager Lǐ’s younger brother, Lǐ Yè, sought to become Commissioner of the Palace Gate.
The Emperor and Empress Dowager privately consulted Bīn about this.
Bīn simply said it was not permissible.
The Emperor wished to make his beloved Lady Gěng Empress,
but Bīn again said it was not permissible.
When Lady Gěng died,
the Emperor planned to bury her with the rites of an empress,
but Bīn again said it was not permissible.
Because of this, Yǐndì was greatly angered,
and his attendants seized the opportunity to sow discord.
He was killed on the same day as Shǐ Hóngzhào and the others.
Bīn was a rather frugal and quiet person.
Although he did not refuse bribes from all corners,
he often presented them to the Emperor.
At home, he refused all guests,
but in his later years, he gradually interacted with literati
and invited guests to his residence.
Knowing the utility of historical records,
he instructed his clerks to copy them.
Not long after,
he met with disaster.
When Zhōu Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he posthumously enfeoffed him as Prince Hóngnóng.
Wáng Zhāng
Wáng Zhāng was
a native of Nánlè in Wèizhōu.
He served as a secretary in the prefecture.
When Zhāng Lìngzhāo expelled the military governor Liú Yánhào,
Wáng Zhāng served Lìngzhāo.
When Lìngzhāo was defeated,
Wáng Zhāng’s father-in-law, Bái Wénkē, was on good terms with the Deputy Commander Lǐ Zhōu,
and entrusted Wáng Zhāng to Lǐ Zhōu.
Lǐ Zhōu hid Wáng Zhāng in a box
and carried him on a camel to Luòyáng,
where he concealed him in his residence.
When the Táng dynasty fell,
Wáng Zhāng emerged
and became the provisions manager for Héyáng.
When Hàn Gāozǔ commanded the imperial guards,
he appointed Wáng Zhāng as a secretary
and Wáng Zhāng followed him to Tàiyuán.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Sānsīshǐ and Jiǎnjiào Tàiwèi.
When Gāozǔ passed away,
Yǐndì ascended the throne,
and Zhāng was promoted to Tàiwèi and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
At this time,
the Hàn dynasty had just been established,
inheriting from the Qìdān.
The capital was impoverished,
and three rebellions broke out in Guānxī.
Zhōu Tàizǔ was campaigning in the west,
and Zhāng supplied the army
without ever running short.
However, he profited from exploiting the lower classes,
which caused great suffering to the people.
Previously, for every shí of grain rent, two shēn were paid as
"quèshǔhào" (sparrow and rat loss);
Zhāng increased this to two dòu per shí as
"shěnghào" (provincial loss).
For money in strings,
all transactions used eighty coins as a mò,
but Zhāng reduced the outgoing amount by three per mò.
When people in the prefectures and counties complained about land,
the entire prefecture and county would be scrutinized
to uncover hidden land.
The empire was thus heavily burdened.
Furthermore, Zhāng particularly disliked scholars.
He once said to someone:
"If you give this sort of person an abacus,
they won't even know how to use it upside down;
what good are they to the country!"
The stipends for all officials were taken from the remnants of military supplies that were unusable.
He ordered the relevant authorities to value them highly,
and after the valuation was set, he would increase it again,
calling it
"yìgū" (forced valuation).
Zhāng was still not satisfied,
and often increased it further.
If people violated laws concerning salt, alum, or yeast,
regardless of the amount, they were sentenced to death.
Officials exploited this for corruption,
and the people could not endure it.
Later, he was killed on the same day as Shǐ Hóngzhào and others.
Liú Zhū
Liú Zhū,
was from Shǎnzhōu.
In his youth, he served as a yájiàng for Liáng Shàowáng.
He had an old acquaintance with Hàn Gāozǔ.
When Gāozǔ was stationed in Tàiyuán,
he made him Zuǒ Dū Yāyá.
Zhū was cruel and fond of killing.
Gāozǔ considered him brave and decisive, like himself,
and particularly trusted and employed him.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
Zhū was appointed Jiédùshǐ of Yǒngxīng Commandery.
He was then transferred to Pínglú,
promoted to Jiǎnjiào Tàishī and Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
and further granted Shìzhōng.
At this time,
the Jianghuai region was inaccessible,
so emissaries from Wúyuè Qián Liú often traveled by sea to reach the central plains.
In all coastal prefectures, Bóyìwù (trade offices) were established
to trade with the people.
If people defaulted or missed deadlines,
the office clerks would arbitrarily arrest and punish them,
setting up their own prisons,
without involving the prefectures or counties.
However, former officials
would accept generous bribes
and let them go unpunished.
The people suffered greatly from this,
so Zhū banned it all.
Nevertheless, Zhū's application of the law
was also excessively harsh.
When people committed an offense,
he would ask their age.
If they answered a certain number,
he would cane them with that many strokes,
calling it
"suíniánzhàng" (age-based caning).
For each person caned,
he would always use two canes simultaneously,
calling it
"héhuānzhàng" (joyful union caning).
He also requested to increase land rent,
charging thirty coins per mù for public use,
which the people could not bear.
Yǐndì was troubled by Zhū's rigidity and violence,
and summoned him,
fearing he would not come.
At this time,
Guō Huái of Yízhōu had returned from attacking Southern Táng
and stationed his troops in Qīngzhōu.
Yǐndì then sent Fú Yànqīng to replace Zhū.
Zhū saw that the imperial guards were present,
and no one dared to have dissenting thoughts,
so he accepted the replacement and returned to the capital.
Zhū had always harbored a bitter grudge against Shǐ Hóngzhào, Yáng Bīn, and others.
Later, when Hóngzhào and the others were killed,
Zhū said to Lǐ Yè and others:
"You gentlemen can truly be called 'lǒulúo'ér' (lowly subordinates)."
While acting as the Prefect of Kāifēng,
Zhōu Tàizǔ's troops invaded the capital.
Zhū executed all the family members of Tàizǔ and Wáng Jùn.
When Tàizǔ entered the capital,
Zhū's wife, naked and covered with a mat,
was captured along with Zhū.
Zhū said to his wife:
"I am going to die,
you will probably become someone's slave."
Tàizǔ sent someone to rebuke Zhū, saying:
"You served the former emperor with me,
do you have no feeling for old friends?
My family was slaughtered and annihilated.
Although it was an imperial command,
the cruelty and venom you added to it,
how could you bear it?
Now you also have a wife and children,
do you think of them?"
Zhū replied:
"I was executing rebellious subjects for Hàn,
I knew nothing else."
At this time,
Tàizǔ was seeking to win over the hearts of the people,
so he discussed with his officials:
"Liu Shìzhōng fell from his horse and was severely injured,
and the soldiers insulted him.
If there is still a slight chance of life,
I wish to propose to the Empress Dowager
to spare his family.
What do you think?"
All the officials thought it was a good idea.
So they ceased killing Zhū,
and impaled his head along with Lǐ Yè and others in the marketplace,
pardoning his wife and children.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he bestowed upon Shǎnzhōu one estate and one residence each.
Lǐ Yè
Lǐ Yè
was the younger brother of Gāozǔ's empress.
The empress had seven siblings,
and Yè was the youngest,
thus particularly beloved.
During Gāozǔ's reign,
he was made Wǔdéshǐ.
When Yǐndì ascended the throne,
due to being the Empress Dowager's relative,
Yè gained even more power
and acted without scruples.
At that time, there was drought and locusts throughout the land,
the Yellow River burst its banks,
and the capital experienced strong winds that uprooted trees
and damaged city gates.
Within the palace, monsters were often seen throwing tiles and stones, and shaking doors.
Yǐndì summoned the Director of Astronomy Zhào Yányì and asked about methods for exorcism.
Yányì replied:
"My duty is to observe celestial phenomena and times,
to notice their changes,
and to examine auspiciousness or inauspiciousness, and nothing more.
Matters of exorcism
are not within my knowledge.
However, what I have heard
is probably the mountain demon (shānxiāo)."
The Empress Dowager then summoned Buddhist nuns to chant scriptures for exorcism.
One nun went to the latrine,
and upon her return,
wept uncontrollably for several days, unaware of people around her.
When she awoke and was questioned,
no one knew the reason.
Meanwhile, the Emperor was close with Yè, Niè Wénjìn, Hòu Zàn, Guō Yǔnmíng, and others,
often exchanging riddles and teasing each other,
and flying paper kites in the palace.
The Empress Dowager repeatedly warned the Emperor about the calamities,
but he did not listen.
Shǐ Yànchāo,
was a man from Yúnzhōu.
He was brave, fierce, and swift.
When Zhōu Tàizǔ rose in Wèi,
Yànchāo was the Commander of the Hàn Lóngjié Army,
and followed with his troops.
When Tàizǔ entered the capital and ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Commander of the Hǔjié Army,
and garrisoned in Jìnzhōu.
Liú Mín attacked Jìnzhōu,
which had no main commander.
The Prefect, Wáng Wàngǎn, was unable to resist.
Yànchāo, with his garrison troops, held out for over a month.
Tàizǔ dispatched Wáng Jùn to relieve it,
and Mín's forces withdrew.
For his功 (gōng), he was promoted to Commander of the Right Flank of the Lóngjié Army,
and also served as Defense Commissioner of Zhèngzhōu.
When Zhōu and Hàn battled at Gāopíng,
Yànchāo served as vanguard,
being the first to climb the ramparts and break the enemy formation.
For this功 (gōng), he was appointed Jìedùshǐ of the Gǎndé Army.
When Zhōu forces besieged Hàn Tàiyuán,
the Qìdān came to Hàn's aid,
emerging from Xīn and Dài.
Shìzōng dispatched Fú Yànqīng to resist them,
making Yànchāo the vanguard.
They fought at Xīnkǒu.
Yànchāo's courage and fury both erupted,
he rode and attacked left and right,
breaking apart and re-engaging several times,
and eventually died in battle.
At this time,
Shìzōng had defeated Hàn at Gāopíng,
and pressed on with his victory.
During the siege of the city,
the generals' opinions were not unified,
and thus no success was achieved for a long time.
Shìzōng wished to withdraw but had not yet decided.
Upon hearing that Yànchāo had died in battle,
he immediately ordered the army to return.
In the haste of the moment,
many lives were lost.
Shìzōng both regretted Yànchāo's death and was frustrated by the lack of success.
He worried and was so vexed that he did not eat for several days.
He posthumously bestowed the title of Tàishī upon Yànchāo,
and generously compensated his family.
Sūn Shèng
Sūn Shèng's original name was Fèng,
and also Jì.
He was a man from Mìzhōu.
He loved learning,
and was skilled in literature,
especially poetry.
When young, he became a Daoist priest,
residing in the Jiǎnjì Palace on Mount Lú.
He often painted the image of the Táng poet Jiǎ Dǎo and placed it on the wall of his room,
revering it morning and evening.
The Daoist priests of Jiǎnjì Palace disliked Shèng,
considering him a sorcerer,
and drove him out with a stick.
Thereupon, he dressed as a scholar and went north to Zhào and Wèi,
where he met Táng Zhuāngzōng in Zhènzhōu.
Zhuāngzōng appointed Shèng as Zuòzuò Zuǒláng.
During the Tiānchéng era,
Zhū Shǒuyīn was garrisoned in Biànzhōu,
and invited Shèng to be his Pànguān.
Shǒuyīn rebelled,
and was executed.
Shèng then abandoned his wife and children,
and fled between Chén and Sòng.
Ān Chónghuǐ disliked Shèng,
believing that Shèng was the one who instigated Shǒuyīn's rebellion.
He had Shèng's portrait painted and offered a reward for his capture,
but could not get him.
Consequently, he exterminated Shèng's family.
Shèng fled to Wú.
At this time,
Lǐ Jǐng was usurping the Yáng family,
and heavily recruited scholars from all directions.
He obtained Shèng,
was pleased with his literary talent,
and had him draft official decrees.
From this, Shèng became well-known.
Shèng was a stutterer,
and could not exchange greetings with people when he met them.
However, once he was seated,
his debates became sharp and eloquent,
and listeners forgot their weariness.
Jǐng especially loved him,
and brought him in for discussions.
Many of his suggestions were to Jǐng's liking,
so he appointed him Yòu Púyè,
and he and Féng Yánjǐ both served as Jǐng's prime ministers.
Shèng regarded Yánjǐ lightly as a person,
often saying:
"Is it acceptable to use a golden bowl and jade cup to hold dog feces?"
Shèng served Jǐng and his son for over twenty years,
reaching the official position of Sīkōng.
His family became increasingly wealthy and arrogant.
Whenever he ate, no tables were set.
He would have many singing girls each hold a dish,
standing in a circle to serve him.
This was called
"meat platters."
People at the time often imitated this.
When Zhōu Shìzōng attacked Huái,
Lǐ Jǐng was fearful.
He first sent Wáng Zhīlǎng, a commander from Sìzhōu, to Xúzhōu,
bearing a letter to seek peace,
but Shìzōng did not reply.
He then sent Hánlín Xuéshì Zhōng Mó and Wénlǐyuàn Xuéshì Lǐ Démíng with a memorial acknowledging himself as a subject,
but still received no reply.
Thereupon, he dispatched Lǐbù Shàngshū Wáng Chóngzhì as Shèng's deputy to present a memorial.
Mó and Shèng and others all stated that Jǐng was willing to cede the six prefectures of Shòu, Háo, Sì, Chǔ, Guāng, and Hǎi,
and pay an annual tribute of a million to aid the army.
However, Shìzōng had already seized Chú, Yáng, Háo, and Sì prefectures,
and wished to take all of Huáinán before stopping.
He therefore detained the envoys and did not send them back,
and attacked Shòuzhōu even more urgently.
Mó and the others saw that Shìzōng was heroic and martial, no match for Jǐng,
and that his army was very strong,
and that Shòuchūn was in danger.
So they said:
"We beg Your Majesty to grant us a five-day reprieve from execution,
and allow us to return to retrieve Jǐng's memorial,
offering all the prefectures north of the Huái River."
Shìzōng agreed,
and sent Gòngfèngguān Ān Hóngdào to escort Démíng and Chóngzhì back south,
while Mó and Shèng were both detained.
After Démíng and the others returned,
Jǐng regretted it,
