“Mào Zhēn has a large territory and a strong army,
and the Táng forces are not yet capable of launching an expedition against him;
Fèng Xiáng is also close to the capital,
making it easy to be endangered and difficult to regret later.
Even if one wished to execute Cháo Cuò to appease the feudal lords at a later date,
I fear it would be impossible.”
Emperor Zhāo Zōng angrily said:
“I cannot sit idly and suffer humiliation!”
He then ordered Ràng Néng to mobilize troops,
and appointed Qín Wáng Sì Zhōu as Western Capital Pacification Commissioner.
When the order was issued,
the people in the capital markets all knew it was unwise
and gathered at Chéng Tiān Mén,
blocking the Chancellor to request not to raise an army.
They threw tiles and stones at the Chancellor.
The Chancellor got out of his carriage and ran,
losing his official seal.
People were greatly alarmed,
but Emperor Zhāo Zōng’s resolve grew stronger.
Qín Wáng led fifty-four divisions of the Imperial Guards to battle at Zhōu Zhì.
The Táng army was defeated and routed,
and Mào Zhēn then invaded the capital,
stationing his troops at Sān Qiáo.
Emperor Zhāo Zōng, from Ān Fú Mén,
killed two Chief Military Commissioners to appease Mào Zhēn
and ordered him to withdraw his troops.
Mào Zhēn had a long-standing grudge against Ràng Néng,
so he said:
“The ones who plotted to raise the army were not the two Chief Military Commissioners,
but Ràng Néng.”
He arrayed his troops at Lín Gāo Yì,
requesting Ràng Néng’s execution.
Ràng Néng said:
“I said it earlier,
only by killing me can the national crisis be relieved.”
Emperor Zhāo Zōng wept, his tears drenching his lapels.
He demoted Ràng Néng to Sī Hù Cānjūn of Léi Zhōu
and granted him death.
Mào Zhēn then withdrew his troops.
The ancient text has "生" (shēng).
The following year,
the Hé Zhōng Jìedùshǐ Wáng Chóng Yíng died,
and his sons Kē and Gǒng contended for the succession.
King Jìn Lǐ Kè Yòng requested Kē be installed,
while Mào Zhēn, along with Hán Jiàn and Wáng Xíng Yú, requested Gǒng be installed.
Emperor Zhāo Zōng did not agree.
Mào Zhēn and others were enraged.
They led the troops of the three commands to invade the capital,
plotting to depose Emperor Zhāo Zōng
and enthrone King Jí, Bǎo.
Before this could be achieved,
King Jìn also raised an army.
Mào Zhēn, in fear,
then killed Chancellors Wéi Zhāo Dù and Lǐ Xī,
leaving his adopted son Jì Péng with two thousand soldiers for imperial guard duties, and departed.
When the Jìn army arrived at Hé Zhōng,
Jì Péng and Xíng Yú’s brother Xíng Shí, among others, vied to abduct Emperor Zhāo Zōng to flee.
The capital fell into great chaos,
and Emperor Zhāo Zōng relocated to Shí Mén.
Mào Zhēn arrived at Hù Xiàn with his troops
and killed Jì Péng to redeem himself.
The Jìn army had already defeated Wáng Xíng Yú
and returned to Wèi Běi,
requesting to attack Mào Zhēn.
Emperor Zhāo Zōng believed that Jìn was distant while Mào Zhēn was near,
and thus wished to protect him as a favor,
hoping that he could be relied upon in times of urgency;
moreover, Mào Zhēn had already killed his son to redeem himself.
Thus, an edict was issued to recall the Jìn army.
Kè Yòng sighed, saying:
“If Táng does not execute Mào Zhēn,
its troubles will never end!”
In the first year of Guānghuà,
Xuē Zhìqín of Lùzhōu died.
Hǎnzhī immediately entered Lùzhōu,
and sent someone to report to Jìn Wáng, saying:
"Zhìqín was about to die,
and the new commander had not yet arrived.
The reason for this
was to guard against other bandits!"
Kèyòng was furious
and dispatched Lǐ Sìzhāo to attack him.
Hǎnzhī seized the Jìn defending generals Mǎ Gài, Yī Tán, and others,
and sent his son Hào to Liáng to beg for troops.
Liáng Tàizǔ sent Dīng Huì to guard Lùzhōu,
and appointed Hǎnzhī as the Jìedùshǐ of Héyáng.
He died of illness
when he reached Huáizhōu,
aged fifty-eight.
Hǎnzhī had initially betrayed Liáng and returned to Jìn.
Jìn Wáng appointed Hǎnzhī to guard Zézhōu,
and Hǎnzhī left his son Qí to associate with Zhuāngzōng,
with whom he was very familiar.
Later, Hǎnzhī betrayed Jìn and returned to Liáng.
Jìn Wáng was angry
and wanted to kill Qí.
Zhuāngzōng gave him a fast horse
and allowed him to flee to Liáng.
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased to obtain Qí and his father,
and had him and Yǒulún lead troops to guard Zhāozōng.
Therefore, during Tàizǔ's time, Qí
always commanded the imperial guard.
When Mòdì executed Yǒuguī,
Qí was involved in the plot.
He was appointed Right Yǔlín Tǒngjūn and Cìshǐ of Chénzhōu.
He served Táng,
successively holding the posts of Cìshǐ of Wèi and Yǎn Prefectures,
and was promoted to Right Lǐngjūn Wèi Shàngjiāngjūn.
He died in the Tiānfú period,
aged seventy,
and was posthumously granted the title of Tàiwèi.
Mèng Fānglì
Mèng Fānglì was
a native of Píngxiāng, Xíngzhōu.
In his youth, he was a soldier,
and was selected as a company commander for his bravery and strength.
In the Guǎngmíng period of Táng,
Gāo Xún, the Jìedùshǐ of Lùzhōu, attacked Zhūgě Shuǎng at Héyáng.
He sent Fānglì to lead troops through Tiānjǐng Pass as the vanguard.
Xún was driven away by his general Liú Guǎng,
and Guǎng was killed by rebellious soldiers.
Upon hearing of the chaos, Fānglì
led his troops from Tiānjǐng and occupied Lùzhōu.
Táng then made him the Jìedùshǐ of Zhāoyì Army.
Zhāoyì controlled five prefectures: Zé, Lù, Xíng, Míng, and Cí,
with its seat in Lùzhōu.
Fānglì believed that Lùzhōu's mountains and rivers were high and perilous,
and its people were strong and fierce.
Since Liú Zhěn, they had often driven away their commanders.
Moreover, he was a native of Xíng,
so he moved his army to Xíngzhōu.
The people of Lù resented Fānglì's relocation,
and consequently submitted Zé and Lù Prefectures to Jìn.
Jìn sent Lǐ Kèxiū to be the Jìedùshǐ of Zéluò.
Fānglì then made Xíng, Míng, and Cí Prefectures his own Zhāoyì Army.
Jìn repeatedly dispatched Lǐ Cúnxiào and others to lead troops to scout Shāndōng.
The people of the three prefectures were almost entirely captured and plundered,
leaving thousands of miles of barren land,
with no one to cultivate or raise silkworms for several years.
Fānglì defended himself with isolated cities,
and sought aid from Liáng.
Liáng was then occupied with affairs in Yǎn and Yùn to the east,
and could not provide help.
In the first year of Wéndé,
Fānglì requested troops from Wáng Róng to attack Jìn,
and Róng agreed.
Fānglì then sent his general Xī Zhōngxìn to attack Jìn's Liáozhōu,
but Róng, due to other reasons, could not send troops.
As the troops failed to keep their appointment,
Zhōngxìn was greatly defeated,
and the Jìn army took advantage of the victory to attack him.
Fānglì's general Shí Yuánzuǒ was
skilled in military matters and very resourceful.
Fānglì had always trusted him.
When Zhōngxìn was defeated,
Yuánzuǒ was captured by the Jìn general Ān Jīnjùn.
Jīnjùn treated him generously
and asked for strategies to attack Xíng.
Yuánzuǒ said:
"Fānglì is good at defense, and Xíng city is strong.
If we attack it,
we will certainly not succeed.
We should quickly attack his Cízhōu.
When Fānglì comes to rescue,
we can defeat him."
Jīnjùn thought this was a good idea.
When they camped west of Fúshuǐ,
Fānglì indeed led troops to rescue,
but was defeated by Jīnjùn.
He galloped back into Xíngzhōu
and closed the city gates, no longer sallying forth.
There were no relief troops from outside,
and food in the city was almost exhausted.
Fānglì went out at night to inspect the city
and shouted orders to the guards,
but the guards did not respond.
Fānglì knew it was hopeless,
so he returned and drank poison, and died.
The army made his younger brother, Míngzhōu Cìshǐ, Qiān, the Liúhòu,
and sought aid from Liáng.
Liáng Tàizǔ sent Wáng Qiányù to lead three hundred cavalry to assist Qiān in defense.
Qiān seized Qiányù and surrendered to Jìn.
Jìn moved Qiān's clan to Tàiyuán,
and appointed him Cìshǐ of Fénzhōu.
Later, he was made Jìedùshǐ of Zéluò.
In the first year of Tiānfù,
Liáng sent Shì Shūcóng to attack Jìn.
He came out of Tiānjǐng Pass,
and Qiān opened the gates and surrendered,
serving as a guide for the Liáng army to attack Tàiyuán,
but they did not succeed.
When Shūcóng's army returned through Lù,
he took Qiān back to Liáng.
Liáng Tàizǔ detested his treachery
and killed him.
Wáng Kē
Wáng Kē was
a native of Hézhōng.
His paternal uncle, Chóngróng,
defeated Huáng Cháo with the Hézhōng army
and rendered meritorious service to Táng.
He was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Hézhōng.
Chóngróng had no sons,
so he adopted his elder brother Chóngjiǎn's son, Kē, as his heir.
When Chóngróng died,
his younger brother Chóngyíng succeeded him.
When Chóngyíng died,
the army then, considering Kē to be Chóngróng's son,
appointed him.
Chóngyíng's sons, Gǒng, the Jìedùshǐ of Shǎnzhōu, and Yáo, the Cìshǐ of Jiàngzhōu,
contested the succession with Kē.
Gǒng and Yáo wrote to Liáng Tàizǔ,
stating that Kē was formerly a servant of the Wáng family,
with the pet name Zhōng'ér,
and should not be allowed to succeed.
Kē also sought aid from Jìn.
The Jìn people reported this to the court,
and Zhāozōng, for Jìn's sake,
agreed.
However, Gǒng and Yáo also allied with Wáng Xíngyú, Hán Jiàn, and Lǐ Màozhēn in the west for support.
Xíngyú and the others submitted joint memorials,
but Zhāozōng replied that Chóngróng and Jìn had rendered great service to Táng,
and since he had already agreed,
it could not be changed.
Xíngyú and the others were enraged,
and used troops to violate the capital,
killing Chancellor Lǐ Xī and others before leaving.
Gǒng and Yáo joined forces to attack Kē in Hézhōng.
Kē sought aid from Jìn,
and the Jìn army marched west to attack the three garrisons.
They proceeded to Jiàngzhōu,
beheaded Yáo, and passed through.
Upon reaching Wèiběi,
they defeated Xíngyú.
Zhāozōng finally appointed Kē as Jìedùshǐ of Hézhōng.
Jìn married a daughter to him,
and sent Lǐ Sìzhāo to lead troops to assist Kē in attacking Gǒng's Shǎnzhōu.
Gǒng was cruel and severe.
He often beheaded people and threw their heads before him,
speaking and laughing as if nothing had happened,
which caused his subordinates great suffering.
The partial general Lǐ Fán, taking advantage of Gǒng's defeat in battle,
killed Gǒng
and declared himself Liúhòu.
At this time,
Liáng had already subjugated Zhèn and Dìng,
and was about to move his troops west.
However, Zhāozōng was deposed by Liú Jìshù,
and the capital was in great chaos.
Cuī Yìn secretly summoned Liáng to bring troops west.
Liáng Tàizǔ, seeing Kē in Héchōng,
feared he would become a problem,
so he turned to Zhāng Cúnjìng and Hóu Yán,
and gave them a large rope,
saying:
"Bind Kē and bring him to me!"
Cúnjìng and his troops marched out of Hánshān,
defeated the two prefectures of Jìn and Jiàng,
and sent Hé Yīn with troops to guard them,
cutting off Jìn's aid.
Cúnjìng besieged Héchōng.
Kē sent an urgent appeal to Jìn,
but Jìn could not advance because of Yīn.
Kē then sent his wife with a letter to Jìn Wáng, saying:
"The bandit's power is such
that we will be begging for food from Liáng morning and evening!
How can Your Excellency bear not to rescue us?"
Jìn Wáng replied:
"Liáng's troops are blocking the way,
and our numbers are unequal.
If we rescue you, Jìn will perish along with you.
It is better for you and Wáng Láng to surrender to the imperial court."
Kē then wrote a letter to Lǐ Màozhēn, saying:
"The Son of Heaven has just returned to power,
and has issued an edict to the vassal towns not to invade each other, in order to pacify the royal house.
Now Duke Zhū has abandoned the agreement and is attacking me;
his ambition will not stop at my humble city.
If my humble city perishes in the morning,
then the northwestern towns will not be able to be held by you gentlemen!
I wish to join Huázhōu in sending troops to Tóngguān to provide support."
Màozhēn did not reply.
Kē, at his wit's end,
then prepared boats on the river,
intending to return to the capital.
Kē ascended the city wall at night to address the defenders,
but the defenders all remained silent.
His adjutant Liú Xùn entered Kē's bedchamber at night to report,
and Kē shouted at him:
"Are the soldiers rebelling?!"
Xùn then removed his outer garment and searched himself before entering, saying:
"If Your Excellency has doubts,
please first cut off my arm!"
Kē said:
"The situation is critical!
What is the plan?"
Xùn said:
"If Your Excellency takes your family and crosses the river at night,
people will certainly fight for boats.
If one man makes trouble,
the great matter will be lost.
It is better to wait until dawn to explain the situation to the army;
those who are willing to follow will still be half.
Otherwise,
we should prepare a surrender document to delay Liáng's troops,
and then slowly plan our allegiance."
Kē thought this was a good idea.
Liáng Tàizǔ, upon submitting to Táng from Tóngzhōu,
immediately relied on Chóngróng.
Because Chóngróng's mother was Lady Wáng,
Liáng Tàizǔ traditionally regarded Chóngróng as his maternal uncle.
Kē then ascended the city wall and called out to Cúnjìng, saying:
"I have a generational friendship with Liáng Wáng.
Your troops should withdraw
and await Liáng Wáng's arrival;
I will then obey his command."
Cúnjìng then withdrew,
and sent a swift messenger to Tàizǔ in Luòyáng.
When Tàizǔ arrived at Héchōng,
he first went east of the city,
wept at Chóngróng's tomb, and then entered.
Kē wanted to appear before Tàizǔ with his hands bound and leading a sheep,
but Tàizǔ said to him:
"How can the kindness of Taishī Ājiù ever be forgotten?
If you, young master, appear in the ceremony of a vanquished state,
what would Taishī think of me?"
Kē met him on the road,
and they clasped hands and sighed.
Then Kē was moved to Biàn.
Tàizǔ, knowing Kē was Jìn's son-in-law,
suspected his disloyalty,
and ordered Kē to go west to pay respects.
When he reached Huázhōu,
he had someone kill him in the relay station.
Zàn
was a son of Chóngyíng.
After Liáng Tàizǔ captured Kē,
he personally took command of Héchōng Jìedùshǐ,
and appointed Zàn as an official.
Zàn served Liáng,
becoming a general of the imperial guards
and the Jìedùshǐ of Tàiníng and Zhènguó Armies.
During Mòdì's reign,
he became the Yin of Kāifēng.
In the fifth year of Zhēnmíng (919 CE),
he replaced Hè Guī as the Commander-in-Chief of the Northern Expeditionary Army.
At this time,
Jìn had already fortified Déshèng.
Zàn crossed the river from Líyáng to attack Chánzhōu,
but failed,
and retreated to Yángcūn,
blocking the upper reaches of the river,
where he was locked in a stalemate with the Jìn people for a year,
engaging in more than a hundred battles, large and small.
Zàn ultimately achieved nothing.
Mòdì sent Dài Sīyuǎn to replace him,
and Zàn returned to being the Yin of Kāifēng.
When Zhuāngzōng entered the capital from Yùn,
Mòdì heard that the Táng troops were approaching,
and wept day and night,
not knowing what to do.
He held the imperial seal himself,
pointed to his palace, and said to Zàn:
"Whether I can keep this
depends on your strategy!"
The Táng troops had already passed Wǎnqú.
Zàn led the city's inhabitants to ascend the walls and resist the defense.
The Táng troops attacked Fēngqiūmén.
Zàn opened the gate and surrendered,
prostrating himself and begging for death.
Zhuāngzōng comforted him and helped him up, saying:
"Our two families have been joined in marriage for generations,
but each subject serves his own lord.
What crime is there?"
He then appointed him Yin of Kāifēng,
and later promoted him to Jìedùshǐ of Xuānwǔ Army.
Soon after, former Liáng officials like Zhào Yán and Zhāng Hànjié were successively executed.
Zàn died of sorrow,
and was posthumously granted the title of Tàizǐ Tàishī.
Zhào Chōu
Zhào Chōu,
his ancestors were from Qīngzhōu.
For generations, they were adjutants in Chénzhōu.
When Chōu was young, he played in the street with other children,
arranging them into ranks,
and giving commands like a general.
Even the older children all obeyed his orders.
His father, Shúwén, saw this
and exclaimed:
"This child will make our family great!"
When he grew up,
he was skilled in archery,
courageous and resolute,
and valued loyalty and righteousness.
The刺shǐ (Prefect) heard of his talent
and summoned him to his command.
He was successively promoted to Dōuyúhòu of the cavalry and infantry of Zhōngwǔ Army.
When Wáng Xiānzhī raided Hénán,
he captured Rǔzhōu
and was about to invade Dōngdū.
Chōu led troops to defeat him,
and Xiānzhī then went south.
Soon after, Huáng Cháo rose up,
and the prefectures and counties everywhere
were often captured by the bandits.
Hundreds of heroes from Chénzhōu
went together to Zhōngwǔ Army,
requesting Chōu to be appointed Cìshǐ (Prefect) to protect themselves.
Zhōngwǔ Army then submitted a memorial recommending Chōu as Chénzhōu Cìshǐ.
Soon after, Cháo captured Cháng'ān.
Chōu told his generals and officials:
"In my estimation,
if Cháo is not executed by the people of Cháng'ān,
he will certainly lead his forces east.
My prefecture will be directly in his path!"
So, he built fortifications for defense,
moved residents within sixty li into the city,
selected their young men,
equipped them with weapons and armor,
and appointed his younger brothers Chǎng and Xǔ as generals.
When Cháo was defeated,
he indeed headed east.
He first sent Mèng Kǎi to occupy Xiàngchéng,
but Chǎng attacked and defeated him,
capturing Kǎi and returning with him.
Cháo arrived later
and was furious when he heard Kǎi had been captured.
Soon after, Qín Zōngquán 宗權 of Cài Zhōu 蔡州 defected to Huáng Cháo 黃巢.
Cháo's 巢's power grew formidable.
He then gathered all his forces to besiege Chén Zhōu 陳州,
setting up grindstones
to grind human flesh for food.
The people of Chén Zhōu 陳州 were afraid.
Chén Zhōu 陳州 said to his subordinates:
"Our family has been generals of Chén Zhōu 陳州 for three generations.
We will surely be able to defend this city.
You men,
you should seek life in death,
achieve great deeds and establish your careers.
It might well be because of this very moment."
All the people of Chén Zhōu 陳州 were encouraged and leaped with joy.
Cháo 巢 built a camp called Bā Xiān Yíng 八仙營 three li north of the city,
erecting palaces,
appointing officials,
and stockpiling provisions,
intending to wear down the city over a long period.
His army numbered two hundred thousand.
The people of Chén Zhōu 陳州 had several hundred giant crossbows,
but they were all broken and in disrepair.
Later-generation crossbow artisans did not even recognize their design.
Chén Zhōu 珍 created an innovative way to repair them.
Crossbow bolts could pierce five hundred paces,
penetrating both men and horses.
For this reason, Cháo 巢 dared not approach.
The siege lasted for three hundred days in total.
When Chén Zhōu 陳 Zhōu's supplies were almost exhausted,
he requested troops from Liáng 梁.
Liáng Tàizǔ 梁太祖 and Lǐ Kèyòng 李克用 both personally led their forces to Chén Zhōu 陳州,
defeating Cháo's 巢's general Huáng Yè 黃鄴 at Xīhuá 西華.
Xīhuá 西華 had accumulated grain,
which Cháo 巢 relied on for provisions.
When Yè 鄴 was defeated,
Cháo 巢 then lifted the siege and departed.
When Liáng Tàizǔ 梁太祖 entered Chén Zhōu 陳州,
Chén Zhōu 陳 Zhōu and his brothers welcomed and paid respects to him at the head of his horse with utmost deference.
However, Chén Zhōu 陳 Zhōu secretly recognized that Tàizǔ 太祖 would surely accomplish great things.
So he humbled himself and yielded,
making plans for self-preservation.
Out of gratitude for Liáng's 梁's aid,
he erected a "living shrine" for Tàizǔ 太祖,
bowing and paying respects morning and evening.
He had his son, Yán 巖, marry Tàizǔ's 太祖's daughter,
who was known as Chánglè Gōngzhǔ 長樂公主.
After Huáng Cháo 黃巢 had departed,
Qín Zōngquán 秦宗權 again caused disturbance in Huaíxī 淮西,
capturing over twenty surrounding prefectures.
Chén Zhōu 陳州 was closest to Cài Zhōu 蔡州,
and Chén Zhōu 陳 Zhōu and his brothers vigorously resisted him,
ultimately preventing him from taking it.
Later, both Cháo 巢 and Zōngquán 宗權 were defeated and died.
Táng Zhāozōng 唐昭宗 then made Chén Zhōu 陳州 the Zhōngwǔ Jūn 忠武軍,
and appointed Chén Zhōu 陳 Zhōu as Jìdùshǐ 節度使.
Chén Zhōu 陳 Zhōu was already ill,
so he ceded his position to his younger brother, Chǎng 昶.
He died a few months later.
Chǎng 昶, taking advantage of the recent suppression of the great bandits,
rested his troops and promoted agriculture,
serving Liáng 梁 with particular diligence.
When Liáng's 梁's troops campaigned in all directions,
Chǎng 昶 supplied provisions and transport,
never slackening.
After Chǎng 昶 died,
Xǔ 珝 succeeded him.
Xǔ 珝 was quite learned.
He sought out the old irrigation works of Dèng Ài 鄧艾,
and breached Zhaíwáng Pí 翟王陂 to irrigate the commoners' fields.
The brothers resided in Chén Zhōu 陳州 for over twenty years,
and the people of Chén Zhōu 陳州 benefited greatly from them.
Liáng Tàizǔ 梁太祖 had already brought Hán Jiàn 韓建 to surrender,
taken Tóng 同 and Huá 華,
and transferred Xǔ 珝 to be Liúhòu 留後 of Tóng Zhōu 同州.
Upon entering Táng 唐,
he became Yòu Jīnwú Wèi Shàngjiāngjūn 右金吾衞上將軍.
After a year or so,
he was dismissed from office due to illness and returned home,
dying at his residence.
The people of Chén Zhōu 陳州 closed their markets in his honor.
Chén Zhōu's 陳 Zhōu's second son, Yán 巖,
served as Hùbù Shàngshū 戶部尚書 and Zūyōng Shǐ 租庸使 during the time of Liáng Mòdì 梁末帝.
He, along with Zhāng Hànjié 張漢傑, Hànlún 漢倫, and others, held power within the court.
Liáng 梁, ever since Tàizǔ 太祖, had been characterized by tyranny and slaughter.
However, Mòdì 末帝 was particularly gentle, soft, respectful, and cautious,
though his nature was mediocre and foolish.
Because Hànjié 漢傑 was his wife's relative,
and Yán 巖 was his son-in-law,
he trusted them implicitly.
The grand ministers and veteran generals all gnashed their teeth,
but Mòdì 末帝 alone did not realize this,
leading to his downfall.
Initially,
Yǒuguī 友珪 killed Tàizǔ 太祖 and established himself,
making Mòdì 末帝 the Dōngdū Liúshǒu 東都留守.
When Yán 巖 went to Dōngdū 東都,
Mòdì 末帝 drank with him,
and calmly revealed his true intentions to him.
Yán 巖 plotted for Mòdì 末帝,

and sent an offer of submission to Lǐ Cóngkē.
Cóngkē sent troops to welcome him.
Wénjìn had governed several prefectures
and often implemented good policies.
The soldiers and people loved him.
When he was about to depart,
he took a few horsemen
and went to the camp himself to bid farewell to his generals and soldiers.
He explained his intention to avoid the Qìdān.
The generals and soldiers all prostrated themselves twice in farewell,
and then he fled south.
Cóngkē appointed Wénjìn as Tiānxíong Tǒngjūn and Xuánrùn Jiéduànshǐ.
Wénjìn was seven feet tall
and had a magnificent appearance.
Since his flight to the Qìdān,
he frequently led the Qìdān to raid and plunder the area between Yōu and Jì,
capturing its people.
He taught the Qìdān Chinese weaving and craftsmanship, making them fully equipped.
The Qìdān became stronger because of this.
During the Tóngguāng reign,
the Qìdān frequently sent Xī cavalry in and out of the passes,
raiding Yān and Zhào.
People had no peaceful years.
Táng troops were stationed in Zhuōzhōu,
and yearly provisions were transported.
From Wǎqiáo Pass to Yōuzhōu,
soldiers were heavily guarded and scouts were deployed,
but they constantly suffered from robbery and plunder.
He was a menace to the Táng for over ten years;
all of this was Wénjìn's doing.
When he fled south,
he began to humble himself and conceal his true nature,
striving to be respectful and cautious.
He courteously received literati,
modest as if he lacked something.
His discussions
were only about recent court ceremonies and stories of the imperial offices,
never mentioning military matters.
Later, he died in Jīnlíng as Zuǒwèi Shàngjiàngjūn.
Lǐ Jīnquán
Lǐ Jīnquán's
ancestors came from Tǔyùhún.
As a youth, Jīnquán was a servant of Táng Míngzōng.
Being brave and skilled in horsemanship and archery,
he often followed Míngzōng in battles.
For his merits, he became a Cìshǐ.
During the Tiānchéng reign,
he served as Jiéduànshǐ of Zhāngyì Jūn.
While in office, he was notoriously greedy and tyrannical.
After his dismissal and return,
he presented several dozen horses.
A few days later,
he presented more.
Míngzōng said to him:
"Are you troubled by too many horses?
Why do you keep presenting them?
And how was your governance in Jīngzhōu?
Surely you were not just preoccupied with horses?"
Jīnquán was ashamed and could not reply.
He was transferred to govern Hénghǎi.
After a long time,
he was dismissed and made Yòuwèi Shàngjiàngjūn.
During Jìn Gāozǔ's time,
Wáng Huī, the Túnfáng Zhǐhuīshǐ of Ānzhōu, killed the Jiéduànshǐ Zhōu Guī.
Gāozǔ sent Jīnquán with a thousand cavalrymen to go there,
and issued an imperial edict inviting Huī to surrender, saying:
"If Huī surrenders,
he shall be made Cìshǐ of Tángzhōu."
He also sent a trusted arrow (a symbol of authority) to Ānzhōu,
declaring that not a single person would be harmed,
and warned Jīnquán, saying:
"Do not break my promise."
Before Jīnquán arrived,
Ān Cóngjìn of Xiāngzhōu, believing Huī would surely flee south of the Yángzi River,
sent elite troops to block his main escape route.
When Huī heard Jīnquán was coming,
he indeed fled south,
and was killed by Cóngjìn's troops.
Jīnquán arrived later
and captured several hundred remnants of Huī's faction,
all of whom he sent to the capital.
During Huī's rebellion,
the city was plundered for three days.
Jīnquán coveted the plundered wealth.
He then arrested and killed more than ten of Huī's generals, including Wǔ Kèhé.
Kèhé shouted:
"Wáng Huī, who started the rebellion,
was still granted an oath of trust
and made a Cìshǐ.
What crime have we committed
that we are to be killed instead?
If this is the court's command,
how can trust be shown?
If the general violates the edict and kills those who surrender,
he too will not escape punishment!"
Gāozǔ could not refute this.
He immediately appointed Jīnquán as Jiéduànshǐ of Ānyuǎn Jūn.
Jīnquán's Zuǒdū Yāyá Míng Hànróng abused his power.
His actions were unlawful.
Gāozǔ was troubled by this
and did not wish to implicate a meritorious official because of Hànróng.
He selected an honest official, Jiǎ Rénzhǎo, to replace him,
and also summoned Hànróng.
Hànróng advised Jīnquán to keep him and not send him away.
Jīnquán's guest, Páng Lìngtú, advised him, saying:
"Rénzhǎo once served Wáng Yànqiú.
When Yànqiú attacked Wáng Dū at Zhōngshān,
Dū sent a skilled archer to ascend the wall and shoot at Yànqiú.
He hit Yànqiú's helmet.
Rénzhǎo drew his bow from behind
and shot the skilled archer.
With one shot, he killed him.
Yànqiú sought the person,
wishing to reward him handsomely,
but Rénzhǎo retreated and said nothing.
This is a loyal minister of the realm.
When Dū was defeated,
Yànqiú sent Rénzhǎo to present the victory report to the capital.
All the rewards he received were very generous,
but he distributed them all among his poor old friends and relatives.
This is an incorruptible scholar of the realm.
A person like this,
how could he plan for others without good intentions?
You should accept Rénzhǎo and send Hànróng away."
When Hànróng heard this,
he sent someone by night to kill Lìngtú and poison Rénzhǎo.
Rénzhǎo's tongue rotted, and he died.
Hóng Zhì, following the command of the deposed emperor, resided in the prefectural office.
Hóng Zhì had a son, Luán.
He was a Diànzhí.
When the deposed emperor was installed,
Luán was dispatched to bring a cup of poisoned wine (zhèn) to Hóng Zhì.
Initially,
Mǐn Dì was in Wèizhōu.
Hóng Zhì ordered a wine merchant from the market to offer wine.
When Mǐn Dì saw it,
he was greatly startled
and immediately collapsed to the ground.
After a long while, he revived.
Hóng Zhì said,
"This is a wine merchant.
He wishes to offer wine to comfort your boredom."
Mǐn Dì accepted it,
and from then on, a cup was offered daily.
When Luán arrived with the poisoned wine,
he had the wine merchant offer it.
Mǐn Dì drank it without suspicion,
and subsequently collapsed and died.
Hóng Zhì later served the Jìn as the Fèngxiáng Xíngjūn Sīmǎ,
and retired as Guānglù Qīng.
When he died,
he was posthumously granted the title of Tàifù.
Liú Shěnjiāo
Liú Shěnjiāo, courtesy name Qiúyì,
was a native of Wén'ān, Yōuzhōu.
In his youth, he had some knowledge of books
and was skilled in official affairs.
He served as the Tángxīng Lìng
and was later appointed to Fànyáng Yákào.
When Liú Shǒuguāng usurped the throne,
he appointed Shěnjiāo as Bīngbù Shàngshū.
After Shǒuguāng's defeat,
he returned to Tàiyuán.
Táng Zhuāngzōng appointed him as a Cóngshì.
Later, Zhào Déjūn took charge of Fànyáng,
and Běimiàn Zhuǎnyùnshǐ Mǎ Shàohóng invited Shěnjiāo to be his Pànguān.
When Wáng Yànqiú campaigned against Wáng Dū,
he was appointed Zhuǎnyùn Gōngjūnshǐ.
After Dìngzhōu was pacified,
he was appointed Cìshǐ of Liáozhōu.
He again served as Běimiàn Zhuǎnyùnshǐ,
then was transferred to Cízhōu Cìshǐ.
He resigned from office due to his mother's old age.
After his mother's death,
his grief and emaciation exceeded proper decorum,
and he remained out of office for several years.
When Jìn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn attacked Fàn Yánguāng in Wèizhōu,
and Shěnjiāo again served as Gōngjūnshǐ.
At this time,
Jìn Gāozǔ divided the Hùbù, Dùzhī, and Yántiě into three separate commissioners.
After more than a year,
the three agencies became increasingly troublesome and inefficient,
so they were combined again into one.
Shěnjiāo was appointed Sānsī Shǐ.
Some counselors proposed inspecting all the cultivated land in the empire
to increase rental income.
Shěnjiāo said,
"There is a fixed quota for rent,
and for many years, there has been no uncultivated land in the empire.
The suffering and happiness of the people
are not equal."
So, the inspection was stopped,
and the people benefited by not being disturbed.
He was promoted to Yòuwèi Shàngjiāngjūn and Chénzhōu Fángyùshǐ.
He went out to inspect the people's fields
and found their farming tools to be crude and inferior.
So, he took farming tools from Hébĕi as models
and had new ones cast for the people.
After Ān Cóngjìn was pacified,
Shěnjiāo was transferred to Xiāngzhōu,
then to Qīngzhōu,
and in both places, he governed well.
He was dismissed and returned.
When the Qìdān invaded the capital,
they left Xiāo Hàn behind and departed.
Hàn again appointed Shěnjiāo as Sānsī Shǐ.
Shortly after, Hàn summoned Xǔ Wáng Cóngyì to guard the capital.
Hàn Gāozǔ raised an army in Tàiyuán.
Cóngyì summoned Gāo Xíngzhōu to resist Gāozǔ,
but Xíngzhōu did not arrive.
Cóngyì's mother, Wáng Shúfēi, consulted with her officials about welcoming Gāozǔ.
Some suggested that since there were still several thousand Yàn soldiers in the capital,
they could defend the city and wait for Xíngzhōu.
Shúfēi disagreed,
and the discussion remained undecided.
Shěnjiāo stepped forward and said,
"I am a native of Yàn.
Now, I am defending the city for Yàn,
and I should plan for Yàn.
However, the circumstances make it impossible to succeed.
Her Highness the Grand Consort's words are correct."
Cóngyì then ceased making preparations
and sent someone west to welcome Gāozǔ.
When Gāozǔ arrived,
he dismissed Shěnjiāo and did not employ him.
During Yǐn Dì's reign,
he served as Rǔzhōu Fángyùshǐ
and gained a reputation for competence.
He died in the third year of Qiányòu (950 CE)
at the age of seventy-four.
The people of Chuān gathered and wept before his coffin,
submitting memorials requesting that he be buried in the nearby suburbs
so that the people could offer sacrifices at the appropriate times each year.
An imperial edict specially posthumously granted him the title of Tàiwèi,
and ordered the erection of a shrine and a stele.
Wáng Zhōu
Wáng Zhōu
was a native of Wèizhōu.
In his youth, he joined the army due to his bravery and strength.
He served Táng Zhuāngzōng and Míngzōng
as a Bìxiào.
For his meritorious service in fierce battles, he was appointed Cìshǐ.
During the Tiānfú reign of Jìn,
he followed Yáng Guāngyuǎn in campaigning against Fàn Yánguāng in Wèizhōu,
and also followed Dù Chóngwēi in campaigning against Ān Chóngróng in Zhènzhōu.
In both instances, he performed meritoriously.
He successively served as Jiédùshǐ of Bèizhōu and Jìngzhōu.
In Jìngzhōu, Zhāng Yànzé had governed harshly and cruelly,
causing many people to flee.
Zhōu then adopted a more lenient approach,
inquired about the people's suffering,
and abolished more than twenty oppressive practices.
All the people returned.
He was successively transferred to the four prefectures of Wǔshèng, Bǎoyì, Yìwǔ, and Chéngdé,
and in all of them, he governed well.
When a bridge in Dìngzhōu collapsed,
overturning the people's grain carts,
Zhōu said,
"The bridge was not repaired;
it is the fault of the Cìshǐ."
So, he compensated the people with grain
and had the bridge repaired for them.
When Dù Chóngwēi surrendered to the Qìdān,
the Qìdān army passed through Zhènzhōu.
They approached the city and called out to Zhōu, urging him to surrender.
Zhōu wept and said,
"Having received profound kindness from the Jìn,
if I cannot die fighting but surrender the city instead,
how can I face the sovereign and the scholar-officials when I go south!"
He then drank heavily,
sought a knife, and wanted to commit suicide.
His family stopped him,
and he was forced to surrender.
The Qìdān appointed Zhōu as the Wǔshèngjūn Jiédùshǐ.
When Hàn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was transferred to govern Wǔníng.
He died in office
and was posthumously granted the title of Zhōngshū Lìng.
Gāo Xíngzhōu (Xíngguī's biography attached)
Gāo Xíngzhōu, courtesy name Shàngzhì,
was a native of Guīzhōu.
His family had for generations been garrison commanders of Huáiróng.
His father was Sījì.
Sījì and his brothers were all renowned in the northern border region for their martial prowess,
serving as garrison commanders under Yōuzhōu Jiédùshǐ Lǐ Kuāngwēi.
When Kuāngwēi was usurped by his brother Kuāngchóu,
the Jìn Wáng was about to suppress the rebellion
and deliberated, saying,
"Gāo Sījì and his brothers are at Kǒnglǐngguān,
with three thousand soldiers.
These will be a future problem.
It would be better to send someone to recruit them.
If Sījì serves us,
then nothing will be impossible."
Kèyòng sent someone to recruit Sījì and his brothers.
The people of Yàn valued loyalty and righteousness.
Sījì and others, hearing that the Jìn army was avenging Kuāngwēi,
joyfully followed them
and became the vanguard of the Jìn army.
Kuāngchóu, hearing that Sījì and his brothers had all defected,
abandoned the city and fled.
Kèyòng appointed Liú Rén'gōng to guard Yōuzhōu,
appointed his eldest brother as Xiānfēng Dūzhǐhuīshǐ,
Sījì as Zhōngjūn Dūzhǐhuīshǐ,
and his younger brother as Hòujūn Dūzhǐhuīshǐ.
The Gāo brothers shared command of the Yàn army.
Kèyòng, upon parting, told Rén'gōng,
"The Sījì brothers
wield influence over an entire region.
Those who will cause trouble for Yàn
will definitely be the Gāo family.
You should guard against them well."
Kèyòng left a thousand Jìn soldiers to guard Rén'gōng.
However, many Jìn soldiers violated the law,
and Sījì and others frequently executed them.
Kèyòng blamed Rén'gōng for this,
and Rén'gōng complained about the Gāo family.
Consequently, Jìn executed all the Sījì brothers.
The Hàn laws were cruel,
and when Shǐ Hóngzhào was in power,
he enjoyed using accusations to kill people.
Jǐngsī had a slave
who once asked for something that was not granted to his satisfaction.
He then rushed to see Hóngzhào,
saying that Jǐngsī was communicating with Lǐ Jǐng
and privately hoarding weapons and armor.
Hóngzhào dispatched an official with thirty cavalrymen to arrest Jǐngsī.
The slave said to the official:
"Jǐngsī is a brave man.
If you get him, kill him;
otherwise, you will lose him."
When the official arrived,
Jǐngsī stepped forward,
embraced the official with both hands, cried out his grievances,
and requested to be sent to prison to explain himself.
The official brought the slave and Jǐngsī together for verification.
Jǐngsī said:
"My house is here;
please search it.
If there are ten thousand cash,
that would be for receiving foreign bribes.
If there is one set of armor,
that would be for privately hoarding weapons."
The official searched it,
and found only a single clothes chest,
military records, and grain registers, nothing more.
The official pitied him and leniently released him.
Jǐngsī requested to be shackled and sent to the capital to clear his name.
Jǐngsī had a servant, Wáng Zhīquán, in the capital.
When Zhīquán heard that Jǐngsī had been accused,
he went to see Hóngzhào,
and volunteered to be imprisoned first to prove Jǐngsī was not rebellious.
Hóngzhào took pity on him,
sent Zhīquán to prison,
and daily provided him with wine and food.
Jǐngsī, already shackled, set off on the road.
The people of Yǐng and Bó followed him to the capital to jointly clear his name.
Hóngzhào then interrogated the slave,
who confessed fully.
He then memorialized for the slave to be executed and Jǐngsī to be released.
Later, he followed Shìzōng in the battle of Gāopíng.
Shìzōng took several thousand surrendered Hàn soldiers and formed the Xiàoshùn Command,
appointing Jǐngsī as its commander.
He was again garrisoned on the Huái River.
When the Zhōu army attacked Huáinán,
he was awarded the title of Ráo Zhōu Cìshǐ for his merits,
and then promoted to Háo Zhōu Cìshǐ.
When the enemy attacked Háo Zhōu,
he died from severe battle wounds,
and was posthumously granted the title of Wǔqīng Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
Wáng Jìn
Wáng Jìn was
a native of Liángxiāng, Yōuzhōu.
He was brave and fierce,
able to run as fast as a galloping horse.
When he was young, he gathered followers and became a bandit,
which troubled the local community.
Fú Yànchāo sent someone to bribe him and recruit him into his command.
When Yànchāo was garrisoned at Ānyuǎn Jūn,
there was a disturbance in the army.
He sent Jìn to quickly report to the capital.
Míngzōng was surprised by his swift arrival,
praised his physical strength,
and assigned him to the Níngwèi Command.
Hàn Gāozǔ was the Shìwèi Qīnjūn Zhīhuīshǐ
and appointed Jìn as a military officer.
When Gāozǔ was garrisoned at Hédōng,
he took Jìn with him.
Whenever there was an emergency,
he would send Jìn to gallop to the capital,
completing the round trip in no more than five or six days.
Because of this, he grew to love and trust him even more,
and he was repeatedly promoted to Fèngguó Jūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ.
He followed Zhōu Tàizǔ when he rose up in Wèi,
and was promoted to Hǔjié Yòuxiāng Dūzhīhuīshǐ.
He successively served as Rǔ and Zhèng Zhōu Fángyùshǐ, and Zhāngdé Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
In the autumn of Xiǎndé 1st year,
he died of illness,
and was posthumously granted the title of Tàishī.

Alas!
When I narrate old histories,
upon reaching the affairs of Wáng Jìn,
I never fail to close the book and sigh, saying: How extreme!
The rulers of the Five Dynasties
all rose from military backgrounds,
and those with whom they associated were brave men and fierce soldiers,
each carving up territory to be enfeoffed as marquises and kings.
How is this different from wolves herding these people?
Although their patronage and opportunities
arose from a temporary stroke of luck,
they still invariably had to expose themselves on the battlefield,
possessing either the bravery of a hundred men
or the merit of a single day's labor.
But for someone like Jìn,
who merely by his swift feet and good running ability came to hold the banner and staff of office,
how exceedingly strange it is!
Is it not that the use of official positions
changes in importance with the times?
When the world is well-governed, gentlemen occupy them and they are valued;
when the world is in chaos, lesser men easily obtain them and they are trivialized?
Or is it that obtaining advantage through chance and good fortune,
though not unheard of,
is especially prevalent in times of chaos,
and when it reaches its extreme,
it results in such cases?
Or could there be even more extreme examples than this?
At this time,
those who ruled a state for a long period governed for no more than ten-plus years;
for a short period, three or four years, or even one or two years.
The people of the world
saw their superiors easily changing rulers and replacing states,
as if merely changing garrisons, no different.
Since it was so trivial,
how much more so for those below them!
As for people like Jìn,
are they even worth mentioning?
As the Yì Jīng says of "Fǒu" (Obstruction) and "Tài" (Peace), flourishing and declining,
gentlemen and lesser men constantly alternate between high and low positions.
Seeing those in high positions like Jìn and his ilk,
one can imagine those below them.
I record Jìn's story
to lament the disorder among these people,
and to show how many worthy and noble men of that time were in low positions!
How many could one possibly count!
How many could one possibly count!
Cháng Sī
Cháng Sī, courtesy name Kègōng,
was a native of Tàiyuán.
Initially, he followed Táng Zhuāngzōng as a soldier,
and later became the Chángjiàn Zhīhuīshǐ.
Through the Táng and Jìn dynasties, he served as Liùjūn Dūyúhòu.
When Hàn Gāozǔ was the Hédōng Jiédùshǐ,
he appointed Sī as the Láochéng Zhīhuīshǐ.
When Gāozǔ entered the capital and ascended the throne,
Sī was made the Wǔshèng Jūn Jiédùshǐ,
and then transferred to govern Zhāoyì.
Sī rose from a military soldier,
never having achieved battle merits.
He merely happened to encounter the rise of the Hàn dynasty
and thus came to hold the banner and staff of office.
He stayed in Lùzhōu for five years,
making wealth accumulation his business,
yet his nature was base and frugal.
Initially,
when Sī was obscure,
Zhōu Tàizǔ was young, an orphan without support,
and ate at Sī's house.
He regarded Sī as his uncle.
Later, Sī and Zhōu Tàizǔ both encountered the Hàn dynasty and attained wealth and status.
After Zhōu Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he always addressed Sī as Uncle Cháng,
and bowed to his wife
with the rites due to family members.
In Guǎngshùn 3rd year,
he was transferred to govern Guīdé.
After residing there for three years, he came to court.
He was then transferred to Pínglú.
Sī then addressed the emperor, saying:
"Your servant resides in Sòng,
and the people of Sòng owe your servant one hundred thousand taels of silk interest.
I wish to present the bonds to Your Majesty."
Tàizǔ nodded,
then immediately burned the bonds,
and issued an edict to Sòngzhōu to cancel all of them.
Sī resided in Qīngzhōu.
More than a year later, he fell ill,
returned to Luòyáng,
and died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Zhōngshūlìng.
Sūn Fāngjiàn
Sūn Fāngjiàn
was a native of Qīngyuàn, Zhèngzhōu.
Initially,
to the northwest of Dìngzhōu, there was Lángshān Fort.
The people of Dìng often took refuge there to avoid the Qìdān.
A nun named Shēnyì resided within it
and attracted people with Buddhist teachings,
many of whom returned to her.
After the nun died,
the fort residents said her body did not decay,
so they revered and served her.
The nun's surname was Sūn.
Fāngjiàn considered himself a relative of the nun
and immediately continued her practices.
The fort residents elected him as their leader.
During the time of Jìn Chūdì,
the Yìwǔ Jūn Jiédùshǐ disliked Fāngjiàn's gathering of followers in the mountains,
fearing he would become a border threat.
Therefore, he memorialized to have him appointed as a Yóuyìshǐ.
Fāngjiàn then sought something which he did not get,
so he allied with the Qìdān to the north.
Later, the Qìdān destroyed the Jìn dynasty
and appointed Fāngjiàn as the Yìwǔ Jūn Jiédùshǐ.
Afterward, they transferred Fāngjiàn to Yúnzhōng.
Fāngjiàn refused the order
and led his followers back into Lángshān.
When Hàn Gāozǔ rose,
the Qìdān set fire to Dìngzhōu,
and carried its people north.
Fāng Jiàn heard of this,
entered from Wángshān,
occupied it, and returned to the Hàn.
Gāozǔ praised him,
and immediately appointed Fāng Jiàn as Jìedùshǐ of Yìwǔ Army.
During Zhōu Tàizǔ's time,
he was transferred to govern Zhènguó,
and his younger brother Xíngyǒu was made Liúhòu of Dìngzhōu.
When Shìzōng attacked Tàiyuán,
Fāng Jiàn paid court at the Emperor's temporary residence,
and followed him back to the capital.
Upon reaching Luò, he fell ill,
and was transferred to govern Kuāngguó.
He died in Luòyáng
at the age of sixty-two,
and was posthumously granted the title of Tàishī.
Collation Notes
Miscellaneous Biographies, No. 38: Wáng Jùn
Wáng Jùn, courtesy name Xiùfēng,
was a native of Ānyáng, Xiàngzhōu.
His father, Fēng,
was a commanding officer of the Le Camp.
When young, Jùn served Liáng Jìedùshǐ Zhāng Jūn by virtue of his good singing.
After Táng Zhuāngzōng had taken Wèibó,
Jūn abandoned Xiàngzhōu
and fled back to the capital.
When Zūyōngshǐ Zhào Yán passed by Jūn's house,
Jūn ordered Jùn to sing to accompany the wine,
and Yán saw him and was pleased.
At this time, Yán was influential,
so Jūn gave Jùn to Yán.
When Liáng fell,
Yán's clan was executed,
and Jùn became a wanderer among the people.
After a long time,
he served Sānsīshǐ Zhāng Yánlǎng,
but Yánlǎng did not favor him much.
When Jìn Gāozǔ destroyed Táng
and killed Yánlǎng,
Hàn Gāozǔ at that time rose in rebellion with Jìn,
and consequently all of Yánlǎng's property was bestowed upon him.
Thus, Jùn came to serve Hàn Gāozǔ.
When Gāozǔ was stationed in Hédōng,
Jùn was a guest general.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Jùn as Kèshěngshǐ.
The Hàn sent Guō Cóngyì to suppress Zhào Sīwǎn,
and appointed Jùn to supervise his army.
He was successively promoted to Xuānhuī Běiyuànshǐ.
When Zhōu Tàizǔ was stationed in Tiānxíong Army,
Jùn served as監軍 (Jiānjūn).
After Hàn Yǐndì had killed Grand Minister Shǐ Hóngzhào and others,
he also sent people to kill Zhōu Tàizǔ and Jùn and others.
Jùn and the others then, with Tàizǔ, raised an army to attack the capital.
When Tàizǔ supervised the state,
by order of the Hàn Empress Dowager, Jùn was appointed Shūmìshǐ.
When Tàizǔ led his troops north,
upon reaching Chánzhōu,
the army turned back towards the capital.
At this time,
Tàizǔ had already sent Féng Dào to welcome Xiāngyīn Gōng Yūn from Xúzhōu,
and the Hàn imperial clan's Càiwáng Xìn was in Xǔzhōu.
Jùn conspired with Wáng Yīn
to send the Shìwèi Mǎjūn Zhǐhuīshǐ Guō Chóng with troops to Sòngzhōu, and former Shēnzhōu Cìshǐ Mǎ Duó to Xǔzhōu to await developments.
Chóng and Duó then killed Yūn and Xìn.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Jùn as Yòupúyè, Ménxiàshìláng, and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì,
and Supervisor of National History.
When Liú Mín attacked Jìnzhōu,
Jùn served as Xíngyíng Dūbùshǔ,
empowered to act as he saw fit.
He separately dispatched Chén Sīràng and Kāng Yánzhǎo to exit from Wūlǐng to Jiàngzhōu to meet Jùn.
When Jùn arrived at Shǎnxzhōu,
he lingered and did not advance.
Tàizǔ sent an envoy, Zhái Shǒusù, to hasten to Shǎnxzhōu
and inform Jùn of his intention to personally lead the campaign.
Jùn dismissed his attendants and said to Shǒusù:
"Jìnzhōu city is strong and cannot be approached,
and Liú Mín's troops are sharp and not yet to be resisted.
The reason I remain here
is not cowardice;
it is because I am waiting for something.
Furthermore, Your Majesty has just ascended the throne,
and the various regional governors
have not yet been brought under your awe and virtue;
how can you act rashly!
Moreover, Mùróng Yànchāo of Yǎnzhōu has already revealed signs of rebellion.
If Your Majesty goes out to Sìshuǐ,
then Yànchāo will enter the capital.
How will Your Majesty deal with him?"
Shǒusù hastened back
and fully recounted Jùn's words.
At this time,
Tàizǔ had already issued an edict to travel west.
Hearing Jùn's words,
he immediately pulled his own ear and said:
"He almost ruined my plan!"
Thereupon, he stopped and did not go.
Jùn's army set out from Jiàngzhōu.
The vanguard reported passing Mēngkēng,
and Jùn was pleased.
He said to his subordinates:
"Mēngkēng
is the strategic pass between Jìn and Jiàng.
Mín did not divide his troops to guard it,
allowing us to pass here.
It is clear that he is bound to be defeated."
When Jùn's army was one shě from Jìnzhōu,
Mín heard that the Zhōu army had arrived in great numbers,
and immediately retreated.
All the generals wanted to pursue him,
but Jùn hesitated, unable to decide.
The next day,
he sent cavalry to pursue Mín,
but they did not catch him and returned.
He participated in the campaign against Mùróng Yànchāo,
serving as Suíjià Dūbùshǔ,
leading the troops to be the first to ascend.
Jùn and Tàizǔ both rose from Wèi,
and he considered his功 as assisting the founding of the dynasty,
taking the responsibility for the empire upon himself.
Whatever he discussed or requested,
regardless of the size of the matter,
he expected to get it.
If it was even slightly not to his liking,
his words and expression were often disrespectful.
Tàizǔ always tolerated him.
Jùn was two years older than Tàizǔ,
and Tàizǔ often called Jùn "elder brother"
or by his courtesy name.
Jùn consequently became even more arrogant.
Zhèng Rénhuì, Lǐ Chóngjìn, Xiàng Xùn, etc.,
were all Tàizǔ's former subordinate generals.
When Tàizǔ first ascended the throne,
he was modest and not yet willing to promote them,
but Jùn was secretly jealous of them.
After returning from defeating Mùróng Yànchāo,
he immediately offered to resign from the Shūmì post to probe the Emperor's intentions.
Tàizǔ comforted and appeased him.
Jùn sent out many letters to the various regional governors,
seeking their endorsement.
After several days,
all the regional governors sent fast riders to present letters to Jùn,
which greatly alarmed Tàizǔ.
Jùn repeatedly submitted memorials requesting resignation
and consequently stopped attending to affairs.
Tàizǔ sent a close minister to summon him, saying:
"If you do not come out,
I will personally go to visit you."
Jùn said:
"If the imperial carriage were to come,
it would bring unforeseen misfortune upon your servant."
However, he showed no intention of coming out.
Shūmì Zhíxuèshì Chén Tóng was on good terms with Jùn.
Tàizǔ immediately sent Tóng to summon Jùn.
Tóng returned and reported:
"Jùn's attitude has somewhat softened,
but he requests Your Majesty to loudly declare that the imperial carriage is being prepared
as if you are about to visit him,
then Jùn will surely come out."
Tàizǔ reluctantly agreed.
When Jùn heard that Tàizǔ was about to come,
he immediately hastened in to pay his respects.
Jùn had built a main hall in the Privy Council office,
which was extremely lavish.
He invited Tàizǔ to visit,
and was greatly rewarded.
Tàizǔ built a small hall in the imperial garden,
and Jùn immediately reported:
"There are already many palaces and houses;
what is the use of this?"
Tàizǔ said:
"There are not a few rooms in the Privy Council office;
why did you also need to build something?"
Jùn was ashamed and unable to reply.
Initially,
when Yànchāo rebelled,
his adjudicant, Cuī Zhōudù, remonstrated, saying:
“Lǔ
is a land of poetry and books.
Since Bóqín, none have been able to dominate as hegemon.
However, many have guarded it with rites and righteousness and maintained their lineage for a long time.
Now, you, Duke, are heroic and mighty,
a hero of your generation.
If you assess your strength and the times before acting,
you can preserve your wealth and status throughout your life.
Lǐ Hézhōng, Ān Xiāngyáng, and Zhènyáng Dù Lìnggōng
are recent examples for reflection.”
Yànchāo was greatly enraged,
but he had no means to harm him immediately.
Later, when he was besieged,
he massively extorted the city's civilian wealth to reward his army.
Yán Hónglǔ, the former Sīmǎ of Shǎnzhōu, feared his flogging
and offered all his family wealth.
Yànchāo believed it was not exhaustive,
and also wanted to punish Zhōudù.
So he ordered Zhōudù to supervise the seizure of Hónglǔ's family assets.
Zhōudù said to Hónglǔ:
“Your life or death
depends on the amount of wealth.
Please do not hide anything.”
Hónglǔ sent his household servants with Zhōudù to dig and search, but found nothing.
Yànchāo then sent Zhèng Lín to press him with a blade.
Hónglǔ, in terror, bowed to his wives and concubines.
His wives and concubines all said there was nothing hidden.
Zhōudù went in to report to Yànchāo,
but Yànchāo did not believe him
and imprisoned Hónglǔ and Zhōudù.
Hónglǔ’s wet nurse found a gold armlet in the mud and offered it to Yànchāo,
hoping to redeem Hónglǔ.
Yànchāo was furious
and sent military officers to flog Hónglǔ and his wife until their flesh was rotten and they died.
Then he executed Zhōudù in the marketplace.
That year, the planet Zhēnxīng violated the constellations Jué and Kàng.
The divination said:
“Jué and Kàng
are the division of Zhèng,
and Yǎnzhōu corresponds to it.”
Yànchāo immediately led his military officials and officers thirty *lǐ* out of the west gate on foot to offer sacrifices,
welcoming it to Kāiyuán Sì,
and sculpted its image to serve it.
He visited it once daily
and also made civilian households erect yellow banners to avert the evil.
Yànchāo was a man of much cunning and fond of accumulating wealth.
While stationed, he once set up a pawnshop.
Some unscrupulous people used fake silver to pawn,
which the chief clerk eventually discovered after a long time.
Yànchāo secretly instructed the chief clerk to bore a hole in the treasury wall at night,
move all the gold and silk to another place, and then report a theft.
Yànchāo immediately posted a notice in the market,
asking people to declare what they had pawned to be reimbursed.
Everyone scrambled to declare their pawned items.
Afterward, those who had pawned fake silver were found,
placed in a deep chamber,
and made to teach more than ten people to work day and night,
all making items with iron as the core wrapped in silver,
which was called
“iron-core silver” (tiě tāi yín).
When he was besieged,
he encouraged those defending the city, saying:
“I have several thousand *dìng* of silver;
I will give it all to you.”
The soldiers privately said to each other:
“This is iron-core stuff,
what good is it again?!”
None would serve him.
The next year, in the fifth month,
Tàizǔ personally led an expedition.
The city fell.
Yànchāo and his wife both threw themselves into a well and died.
His son, Jìxūn, led his five hundred followers and fled but was captured.
His clan was then exterminated.
When Yǎnzhōu was pacified,
Tàizǔ issued an edict posthumously granting Yán Hónglǔ the title of Zuǒ Xiāowèi Dàjiāngjūn, and Cuī Zhōudù that of Mìshūjiān.
Collation Notes
Miscellaneous Biographies, Forty-Second
The *zhuàn* says:
“Rites, righteousness, integrity, and shame
are the four pillars of the state.
If the four pillars are not extended,
the state will perish.”
How excellent
Guǎn Shēng’s words are!
Rites and righteousness
are the great laws for governing people;
integrity and shame
are the great principles for establishing oneself.
Indeed, if one lacks integrity,
there is nothing one will not take;
if one lacks shame,
there is nothing one will not do.
If a person is like this,
then calamity, chaos, ruin, and destruction
will also be all-encompassing.
How much more so if one is a high minister who takes and does everything,
then how can the world not be in chaos,
and how can the state not perish!
When I read FÉNG Dào’s *Chánglè Lǎo*,
I saw him describe himself as glorious,
which can be said to be utterly shameless.
From this, the state of the world can be understood.
Among the Five Dynasties, I found three individuals of complete integrity
and fifteen ministers who died for their cause.
Yet, I am surprised that many scholars, dressed as Confucians and claiming to study the ancients,
who enjoyed people’s salaries and held positions in their states,
allowed the virtues of loyalty and righteousness
to appear solely among military men and common soldiers.
Could it be that among scholars, there were truly no such people?
Or could it be that noble-minded individuals detested the chaos of the times,
scorned their era, and were unwilling to serve?
Or were the rulers of the world not worth considering,
and thus unable to attract them?
Confucius said:
“In a town of ten households,
there will surely be those who are loyal and trustworthy.”
How could this be an empty statement!
I once obtained a short story from the Five Dynasties period,
which recorded the deeds of WÁNG Níng’s wife, Lǐ Shì.
That even a woman could be like this
shows that such people indeed existed in the world but were not seen.
Níng’s family lived between Qīng and Qí.
He served as the Sīhù Cānjūn of Guózhōu
and died in office from illness.
Níng’s family was always poor.
His son was still young.
Lǐ Shì carried her son
and bore his remains back home.
Passing east through Kāifēng,
she stopped at an inn.
The innkeeper, seeing a woman traveling alone with a child, suspected her
and refused her lodging.
Lǐ Shì, seeing it was already dusk,
refused to leave.
The innkeeper pulled her arm to put her out.
Lǐ Shì looked up to heaven and wailed:
“I am a woman,
unable to preserve my chastity,
and yet this hand has been grabbed by a man?!
I cannot let one hand contaminate my whole body!”
She immediately took an axe and cut off her own arm.
Passersby who saw it gathered around, lamenting her,
some snapping their fingers in dismay,
others shedding tears for her.
The Yǐn of Kāifēng heard of it
and reported the matter to the court.
The officials granted medicine to seal her wound
and amply compensated Lǐ Shì,
while flogging the innkeeper.
Alas,
may those gentlemen who do not cherish themselves and endure shame to cling to life
feel a little shame upon hearing the story of Lǐ Shì!
FÉNG Dào
FÉNG Dào, courtesy name Kědào,
was a native of Jǐngchéng, Yíngzhōu.
He served Liú Shǒuguāng as a Cānjūn.
When Shǒuguāng was defeated,
he left to serve the eunuch Zhāng Chéngyè.
Chéngyè supervised the Hédōng army
and made him an巡官 (Xúnguān).
He recommended him to the King of Jìn for his literary talent,
where he became the Zhǎngshūjì of Hédōng Jiédù.
When Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne,
he was appointed Hùbù Shìláng
and concurrently Hànlín Xuéshì.
During the Chángxīng reign,
Emperor Fèi lost Hèzhōng,
and was dismissed to reside in Qīnghuà Fāng.
He was in the same alley as Qí,
and Qí often went to visit him.
Later, Emperor Fèi ascended the throne,
treating Qí very favorably.
He was appointed Zhī Zhìgào, Gěishì Zhōng, Shūmìyuàn Zhíxuèshì, and Duānmíngdiàn Xuéshì.
At this time,
Jìn Gāozǔ was stationed in Hédōng,
and harbored ulterior motives.
Emperor Fèi worried about this,
and Qí and Lǐ Sōng were both on call for consultation,
offering much beneficial planning.
Qí said:
“The trouble in Tàiyuán
will surely involve the Qìdān for assistance.
It is better to preemptively control it.”
Ever since Wáng Dū rebelled in Dìngzhōu during Míngzōng’s time,
the Qìdān had sent Tūněi, Cuòlà, and others to assist Dū.
However, they were defeated by Zhào Déjūn and Wáng Yànqiú.
Tūněi was killed,
and Cuòlà and others were all sent to the capital.
Thereafter, the Qìdān repeatedly sent envoys to request the return of Cuòlà and others,
their words being very humble and respectful.
Míngzōng invariably executed their envoys and did not reply.
Moreover, Dōngdān Wáng fled into China.
Because of this, the Qìdān frequently sought peace.
Qí then said:
“Given the current situation,
it is better to establish peace with the Qìdān.
Following the precedent of the Hàn dynasty,
we should annually provide gold and silk,
and marry off a daughter to them,
so that powerful vassal states and great garrisons will have no external allies to draw upon,
which can quell their rebellious intentions.”
Sōng conveyed Qí's words to Sānsī Shǐ Zhāng Yánlǎng.
Yánlǎng said joyfully:
“If it can alleviate the nation's troubles,
even if the state expends tens of thousands of strings of cash annually,
charging me to make up the difference would be acceptable!”
They then jointly proposed the matter.
Emperor Fèi was greatly pleased.
Another day, he asked Shūmì Zhíxuèshì Xuē Wènyù about Qí’s and others’ proposal.
Wènyù strongly deemed it wrong,
and then recited Róng Yù's
poem, “The altars of soil and grain rely on an enlightened ruler,
safety and danger are entrusted to a woman,”
to criticize Qí and the others.
Emperor Fèi became furious,
and urgently summoned Sōng, Qí, and others, asking how their plan for peace with the barbarians was.
Perceiving the emperor’s angry expression,
Qí and others quickly said:
“Your ministers’ plan for the nation
is not to seek profit for the Qìdān from China.”
The emperor immediately erupted in anger, saying:
“Do you, my lords, assist me wishing to achieve great peace in such a manner?
I have one daughter who is still young,
and you wish to abandon her to the barbarians?
Gold and silk are for supporting soldiers and defending the nation,
yet you would give them to aid the enemy?
Is that permissible?”
Sōng and the others, terrified, bowed in apology,
bowing countless times.
Qí, due to fatigue in his legs,
could not continue bowing and stopped first.
The emperor said:
“Lǚ Qí is stubborn;
does he consider me a mere person?”
Qí replied:
“Your minister has always been frail,
and is exhausted from too much bowing.
Please allow your minister a short rest.”
After a moment, his breathing settled,
and he reported:
“If Your Majesty deems your ministers' words incorrect,
you may punish them.
What good is bowing?”
The emperor's anger slightly subsided,
saying:
“No need to bow.”
He bestowed a cup of wine and dismissed them,
and the proposal was subsequently dropped.
Consequently, Qí was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
After residing there for several months,
he was again made Duānmíngdiàn Xuéshì.
Later, Jìn Gāozǔ rose up in Tàiyuán,
and indeed brought in the Qìdān for assistance,
thus causing the fall of the Táng dynasty.
Qí served the Jìn dynasty as Mìshū Jiān,
and was successively promoted to Bīngbù Shìláng.
He died in Tiānfú eighth year.
Zhào Yù served as Zhífāng Yuánwàiláng.
Qí treated him like a father.
When Yù was ill,
Qí personally tasted his medicine and attended to him.
When Yù died,
Qí managed the funeral arrangements for his family.
Yù’s son, Wéndù, was orphaned young.
Qí taught him to study,
as if he were his own son.
Later, Wéndù passed the imperial examination as a *jìnshì*.
Qí had sons Yúqìng and Duān.
Xuē Róng
Xuē Róng
was a native of Píngyáo, Fénzhōu.
In his youth, he was renowned for his Confucian scholarship.
During the reign of Táng Míngzōng, he served as Yòubǔquē,
and was concurrently a scholar in the Hóngwén Guǎn.
When Jìn Gāozǔ was stationed in Tàiyuán,
Róng served as Guānchá Pànguān.
When Gāozǔ was transferred to Yùn,
he wished to hold Tàiyuán and defy the imperial command.
He met with his aides and subordinates,
asking them for their opinions.
Among those present, some supported him,
while others were too afraid to speak.
Róng alone calmly replied:
“Róng is merely a Confucian scholar;
I have never studied military affairs.
How can the principles of advance, retreat, survival, and destruction be easily spoken of?”
Gāozǔ did not reprimand him.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
Róng was appointed Lìbù Lángzhōng,
concurrently Shìyùshǐ Zhī Záshì.
He was successively appointed Zuǒ Jiànyì Dàfū,
and then promoted to Zhōngshū Shèrén.
Róng said:
“Literary composition is not my forte.”
He then declined the appointment and did not accept it.
At that time, an imperial edict ordered the repair of the Luòyáng Dàinèi.
Róng submitted a memorial of strong remonstrance.
Gāozǔ praised and accepted his words,
and immediately issued an edict to cease the project.
He was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
then transferred to Shàngshū Yòuchéng,
and assigned to Fēnsī Xī Jīng.
He died
at the age of sixty.
Hé Zé
Hé Zé
was a native of Guǎngzhōu.
His father, Dǐng,
served as Róngguǎn Jīnglüèshǐ at the end of the Táng dynasty.
Zé was fond of learning in his youth
and excelled in poetry.
He passed the imperial examination as a *jìnshì*
and became Luòyáng Lìng.
Táng Zhuāngzōng was fond of hunting
and often trampled on people's fields.
Zé secretly hid in the weeds to wait for Zhuāngzōng.
He intercepted the emperor's horse and remonstrated, saying:
“Your Majesty has not yet unified the realm to cease warfare,
yet you oppress and exhaust the people with heavy taxes to supply the army.
Now the fields are nearing harvest.
How can you indulge in hunting and harm the abundant crops?
How will the people pay their taxes,
and how will officials urge them to farm?
If Your Majesty does not listen to your minister's words,
I beg to be granted death before your horse,
so that future generations may know of Your Majesty's transgressions.”
Zhuāngzōng laughed heartily
and ceased his hunting for his sake.
Zé was appointed Cāngbù Lángzhōng.
During Míngzōng’s reign,
he repeatedly submitted memorials on current affairs.
When Míngzōng visited Biànzhōu,
he also wished to visit Yè,
but public sentiment was against it.
High officials repeatedly advised against it, but he did not listen.
Zé prostrated himself before the palace gate and remonstrated strongly.
Míngzōng praised him
and appointed him Lìbù Lángzhōng and Shǐguǎn Xiūzhuàn.
Though Zé spoke frankly externally,
he was actually insidious and obsequious internally.
Once, during an inner court audience,
after the assembly retired,
he alone remained.
He tapped his forehead with his tablet,
looked north, and cried out:
“Enlightened ruler!
Enlightened ruler!”
All who heard him laughed at him.
During the Fìve Dynasties period,
the people suffered from warfare.
Often, claiming parental illness, they would cut off a piece of their flesh,
or after a parent's death, cut their breasts or reside in a hut by the tomb,
to seek exemption from prefectural and county taxes and labor service.
The Hùbù annually issued countless exemption certificates,
and ordered prefectures and counties to provide paper,
which was called
“exemption paper.”
Zé submitted a memorial detailing its abuses, and Míngzōng issued an edict to abolish all Hùbù exemption paper.
ZÉ had an old acquaintance with Prime Minister Zhào Fèng.
He frequently made private requests to Fèng,
asking to be a Supervising Remonstrator.
Fèng thought little of his character,
and appointed him Grand Court أقلل 少卿 (Tàicháng Shàocīng).
Before the imperial edict was issued, Zé knew about it in advance.
He immediately claimed his new office and submitted a memorial of self-recommendation.
The memorial was sent down to the Central Secretariat.
Fèng and others said:
"Zé claimed his new office before receiving the official appointment,
which is an insult to the court.
We request that he be punished according to the law."
He was then made Grand Coachman 少卿 (Tàipú Shàocīng) and retired,
residing in Héyáng.
Zé was already seventy years old at the time,
but still hoped for official advancement.
He sent his maid Yízǐ to the suggestion box to submit a memorial discussing affairs,
requesting the establishment of Qín Wáng as crown prince.
Qín Wáng was inherently arrogant
and often harbored rebellious intentions.
This eventually led to his downfall,
and it began with Zé.
When Jìn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
Zé was summoned to be Grand Court 少卿 (Tàicháng Shàocīng),
but he died of illness at home.
WÁNG Quán
WÁNG Quán, courtesy name Xiùshān,
was a native of Tàiyuán.
He was the great-grandson of Táng Zǔ Púyè Qǐ.
His father, Ráo,
held the office of Yòusī Lángzhōng.
Quán passed the imperial examination for jinshi,
and became Yòu Bǔquē.
When the Táng dynasty fell,
he served Liáng as Zhífāng Yuánwàiláng, Zhī Zhìgào, and Hàlín Xuéshì,
and was successively promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
When Táng Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng,
Quán was demoted to Suízhōu Sīmǎ.
He was later recalled to be Yòu Shùzǐ,
and successively promoted to Hùbù Shàngshū.
During the reign of Jìn Gāozǔ, he was Bīngbù Shàngshū.
At this time,
Gāozǔ treated the Qìdān as a father.
Quán was to be dispatched as an envoy.
He sighed and said:
"Although I am untalented,
how can I bow before the yurts?"
He therefore declined to go,
and for this reason, he was suspended from his post.
A year later, he retired as Tàizǐ Shàofù.
He died
at the age of seventy-eight,
and was posthumously granted Zuǒ Púyè.
SHǏ Guī
SHǏ Guī
was a native of Shíyì, Chángshān.
He was intelligent, astute, and fond of learning.
As the magistrate of Níngjìn and Lèshòu counties,
he governed well,
and the county people erected steles to praise him.
When Guō Chóngtāo garrisoned Chéngdé,
he appointed Guī as his aide.
During Míngzōng's reign,
he served as Shàngshū Láng.
When Ān Chónghuì became Pímìshǐ,
he recommended Guī to be Zhí Xuéshì.
According to custom,
although the position of Zhí Xuéshì was esteemed,
he was responsible for receiving and handling documents,
and participating in various administrative affairs,
no different from a Pànguān.
Chónghuì was not well-read,
and relied on Guī for consultations.
He first obtained permission for Guī to ascend the hall and attend.
The custom of Pímì Zhí Xuéshì ascending the hall began with Guī.
He was later changed to Shàngshū Yòuchéng,
and put in charge of the personnel selection of the Ministry of Personnel.
When Chónghuì was defeated and died,
Guī was sent out as Bèizhōu Cìshǐ.
After being dismissed, he returned to Chángshān,
cut off all social interaction,
and traveled in a covered carriage when going out in the neighborhoods.
When Jìn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,

and its territory was divided to establish Jìnghǎi and Hǎimén two counties as its subordinates, and its seat was in Jìnghǎi.
Jūnzhōu,
established by Southern Táng Lǐ Jǐng.
Gāo'ān, Shànggāo, Wànzǎi, and Qīngjiāng four counties from Hóngzhōu were assigned as its subordinates, and its seat was in Gāo'ān.
Jiànzhōu,
established by Southern Táng Lǐ Jǐng,
Yánpíng, Jiànpǔ, and Fùshā three counties from Jiànzhōu were assigned as its subordinates, and its seat was in Yánpíng.
Quánzhōu,
established by Chǔ Wáng Mǎ Xīfàn.
Xiāngchuān county from Tánzhōu was renamed Qīngxiāng county,
and Guànyáng county was also assigned as its subordinate, and its seat was in Qīngxiāng.
Xiùzhōu,
established by Wúyuè Wáng Qián Yuánguàn.
Jiāxīng county from Hángzhōu was assigned as its subordinate, and its seat was there.
Xióngzhōu,
established by Southern Hàn Liú Yǎn, assigning Bǎochāng from Sháozhōu,
its seat was in Bǎochāng.
Yīngzhōu,
established by Southern Hàn Liú Yǎn, assigning Zhēnyáng from Guǎngzhōu,
its seat was in Zhēnyáng.
Kāifēng Fǔ formerly governed six counties.
In the first year of Liáng Kāipíng,
Suānzǎo and Chángyuán from Huázhōu,
Zhōngmóu and Yángwǔ from Zhèngzhōu,
Xiāngyì from Sòngzhōu,
Kǎochéng from Cáozhōu (renamed Dàiyì),
Fúgōu and Líng from Xǔzhōu,
and Tàikāng from Chénzhōu were subordinated to it.
Táng returned Suānzǎo, Zhōngmóu, Xiāngyì, Líng, and Tàikāng five counties to their former affiliations.
Jìn promoted Biànzhōu to Dōngjīng,
and again subordinated these five counties to it.
Yōngqiū,
Jìn renamed it Shí,
Hàn restored its former name.
Chángyuán,
Táng renamed it Kuāngchéng.
Líyáng,
formerly belonged to Huázhōu,
Jìn assigned it to Wèizhōu.
Yè and Xiāngchéng,
formerly belonged to Xǔzhōu,
Táng assigned them to Rǔzhōu.
Chǔqiū,
formerly belonged to Shànzhōu,
Liáng assigned it to Sòngzhōu.
Mìzhōu Jiāoxī,
formerly called Fǔtáng,
Liáng renamed it Ānqiū,
Táng restored its former name,
Jìn renamed it Jiāoxī.
Wèinán,
formerly belonged to Jīngzhào,
Zhōu reassigned it to Huázhōu.
Tóngguān,
formerly belonged to Jīngzhào Fǔ,
Liáng assigned it to Tóngzhōu,
Táng assigned it to Yàozhōu.
Měiyuán,
formerly belonged to Tóngzhōu,
Lǐ Màozhēn established Dǐngzhōu and governed it.
Liáng renamed it Yùzhōu,
subordinate to Shùnyì Jūnjiédù.
Later, its abolition time is not seen.
In the third year of Táng Tóngguāng,
it was assigned to Yàozhōu.
Zōngbì,
whose original surname was Wèi,
was named Hóngfū.
Wáng Jiàn adopted him as a son.
When Jiàn attacked Gù Yànhuī,
Zōngbì often leaked Jiàn's plans to Yànhuī.
After Yànhuī was defeated,
Jiàn treated him as before.
When Jiàn fell ill and was about to die,
Zōngbì held the positions of Grand Preceptor (tàishī) and concurrent Director of the Central Secretariat (zhōngshūlìng), and Administrator of the Six Armies (pàn liùjūn),
assisting in governance.
After Wáng Yǎn had surrendered,
Zōngbì offered the treasures of Shǔ to Wèi Wáng and Guō Chóngtāo,
requesting to be appointed Military Governor of Xīchuān (Xīchuān Jiédùshǐ).
Wèi Wáng said:
“These are my family's possessions,
why present them as offerings?”
A few days later,
he was killed by Chóngtāo.
Zōngshòu
was a commoner from Xǔzhōu.
Jiàn adopted him as a son
because they shared the same surname.
Zōngshòu was fond of learning,
skilled in playing the qín and in chess,
and was quiet and retiring by nature.
He enjoyed Daoist arts.
When he served Jiàn, he was the Military Governor of Zhènjiāng Commandery (Zhènjiāngjūn Jiédùshǐ).
After Yǎn was enthroned,
Zōngshòu became Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (tàizǐtàibǎo) and attended court (fèng cháoqǐng),
amusing himself with alchemy and nurturing his vital energy.
Yǎn engaged in lewd and disorderly conduct,
and Zōngshòu alone often remonstrated with him sharply.
Later he became Military Governor of Wǔxìn Commandery (Wǔxìnjūn Jiédùshǐ).
When the Táng army attacked Shǔ,
local areas surrendered upon their arrival,
and Wèi Wáng even sent letters to invite him to surrender.
Only Zōngshòu refused to surrender.
When he heard that Yǎn had already surrendered with the jade disk in his mouth (xiánbì),
he wept greatly.
He followed Yǎn on his eastward migration.
Upon reaching Qíyáng,
he bribed the guards
and was able to see Yǎn.
Yǎn cried until his lap was soaked,
saying:
“If I had listened to your words earlier,
how could I have come to this today!”
After Yǎn died,
Zōngshòu fled to Miǎnchí.
When he heard that Zhuāngzōng had been assassinated,
he disappeared into Mount Xióng'ěr.
In the second year of Tiānchéng (927 CE),
he emerged and went to the capital,
submitting a memorial to request burial for Yǎn's clan.
Míngzōng praised his loyalty
and appointed him as Assistant Military Administrator (xíngjūn sīmǎ) of Bǎoyì Commandery (Bǎoyìjūn),
enfeoffed Yǎn as Shùnzhèng Gōng,
and permitted him to be buried with the rites of a feudal lord.
Zōngshòu obtained the coffins of eighteen members of the Wáng family
and buried them in Sānzhào Village, south of Cháng'ān.
Alas!
Since the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
scholars have largely spoken of auspicious omens (xiángruì).
Even those skilled in discernment
could not dispel their delusion!
When I read the History of Shǔ,
regarding turtles, dragons, qílín, phoenixes, and zōuyú – what the world calls the auspicious omens of a king –
none failed to appear in their state.
How extraordinary!
However, by examining why the Wáng family rose and fell, succeeded and failed,
one can understand it.
Some might think that a single Wáng family is insufficient to account for this;
then by observing the order and disorder of the world at that time,
one can understand it.
As for the dragon,
it is considered divine by not being seen,
and by ascending into the clouds and traveling through the heavens it achieves its ambition.
Now, it lies prone, its form exposed –
this is not divine;
it does not ascend to heaven but appears below in the water –
this is a dereliction of duty.
Yet, how numerous they were!
They can be considered omens of disaster!
The phoenix
is a bird that stays far from humans.
In ancient times, when Shùn governed the world,
his administration was perfected and the people were pleased.
He ordered Kuí to compose music.
When the music was harmonious,
birds and beasts all danced upon hearing it.
At that time,
a phoenix happened to arrive.
Shùn's historian consequently recorded it as a marvel,
and later generations therefore took the arrival of a phoenix as a sign of a virtuous reign.
Thereafter, phoenixes appeared many times,
sometimes during the reigns of mediocre rulers and misguided policies,
sometimes during periods of peril, destruction, and great chaos.
Are these truly auspicious omens?
The qílín
is a beast that stays far from humans.
In ancient times, when Lǔ Āigōng went hunting,
he caught one but did not recognize it.
It was sought out and captured,
not something that appeared on its own.
Therefore, Confucius wrote in the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū),
“Westward hunt and captured a qílín” –
this
was a criticism.
“Westward hunt”
means it was not far;
“captured a qílín”
means he disliked his exhaustive taking.
A hunt must record the place,
but Āigōng traversed many places during his pursuit,
so they could not all be named individually.
Therefore,
“west”
was written to encompass all the lands,
meaning he reached everywhere west of his state.
The qílín
is a beast rarely recognized by humans.
Its appearance shows that the Duke exhausted mountains and drained marshes to take everything,
even to the point of searching for and capturing
beasts he did not recognize.
Thus, it is said
“this was a criticism.”
After the Sages passed away,
heterodox theories arose,
and then the qílín was taken as an omen of a king,
and attached to it were portents, prophecies, and strange, bizarre sayings.
A phoenix once appeared during Shùn's time
and was considered an omen,
which still makes some sense.
But when it later appeared in times of chaos,
then one can know it was not an omen.
As for the qílín,
in previous well-governed eras like those of Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, Wǔ, and Zhōugōng,
it never once appeared.
Its single appearance occurred during a chaotic era.
Therefore, who knows if it was an omen?
The turtle
is a creature of mystery.
In muddy rivers and marshes,
they are countless.
Its value to diviners after its death
is simply due to its suitability for that purpose.
But in Dài's Rites (Dài Lǐ), its presence in palace ponds is considered a rare omen for a king,
and Dài Lǐ contains various contributions from different schools,
so its errors are also numerous!
As for the zōuyú,
I do not know what kind of creature it is.
The Shījīng says:
“Alas for the zōuyú!”
Jiǎ Yì believed that zōu
referred to Wénwáng's park,
and yú
referred to the park official (yúguān).
At the time of Yì,
this explanation was current.
Then, to consider it a beast –
did that explanation originate in recent times?
Indeed, dispelling people's delusions
is difficult to debate during times of strong belief.
One must wait until they harbor some doubt,
and then one can proceed to attack it.
The qílín, phoenix, turtle, and dragon,
considered omens of a king,
appeared during the period of the Five Dynasties,
and moreover were all concentrated in Shǔ.
Even those who are fond of speaking of auspicious omens should find this questionable.
By attacking what is questionable,
perhaps the deluded will be prompted to think.

According to the Former Shǔ History (Qián Shǔ Shū), the Yùnlì Tú, and the Jiǔ Guó Zhì, all state that Jiàn entered Chéngdū in the second year of Dàshùn of Táng and became Military Governor of Xīchuān,
and in the seventh year of Tiānfù, in the ninth month, he proclaimed himself emperor,
and in the first month of the following year, he changed the era name to Wǔchéng.
This is now taken as definite.
Only the Old History of the Five Dynasties (Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ) states,
“He entered Chéngdū in the first year of Lóngjì,
and proclaimed himself emperor and changed the era name in the fifth year of Tiānyòu,”
which is erroneous.
Regarding the fall of Shǔ in the third year of Tóngguāng of Later Táng,
all records agree.
From the second year of Dàshùn to the third year of Tóngguāng,
there were thirty-five years in total.
