Fourth Chapter on the Later Shǔ Imperial Family: Mèng Zhīxiáng (and his son Mèng Chǎng)
Shùlǜ was intelligent and patient.
When Ābǎojī died,
she summoned all the wives of the generals who had accompanied him,
and said to them:
"I am now a widow;
how can you all still have husbands?"
She then killed over a hundred of his generals,
saying:
"You may go and attend the late emperor."
If any of her attendants erred,
many were sent to Mùyè Shān,
and killed in Ābǎojī's tomb passage,
saying:
"Go see the late emperor for me in the underworld."
General Zhào Sīwēn
was originally a man from Zhōngguó,
and was favored by Ābǎojī for his talent and bravery.
Later, Shùlǜ became angry with him over an issue,
and ordered him to be sent to Mùyè Shān.
Sīwēn refused to go,
whereupon Shùlǜ said:
"You,
a trusted confidant of the late emperor,
how can you not go to see him?"
Sīwēn replied:
"No one is closer than Your Majesty the Empress Dowager;
why do you not go?"
Shùlǜ said:
"I originally intended to follow the late emperor to the underworld,
but because my son is young
and there are many troubles in the state,
I have not been able to.
However, I can cut off one of my arms and send it."
Her attendants earnestly remonstrated,
so she cut off one of her wrists,
and released Sīwēn, not killing him.
Initially,
when Déguāng attacked Jìn,
Shùlǜ often disapproved,
saying:
"Is it acceptable for our country to have a Hàn person as its ruler?"
Déguāng said:
"No, it is not."
Shùlǜ said:
"If so, then you, having gained Zhōngguó, cannot hold it.
Later there will certainly be disaster,
and regret will be too late."
When Déguāng died,
his body was transported back.
Shùlǜ did not weep but stroked his corpse and said:
"Wait until my people and livestock in the country are as before,
then I will bury you."
Later,
Wùyù imprisoned her,
and she later died at Mùyè Shān.
Wùyù changed his name to Ruǎn,
and was styled Tiānshòu Huángdì,
changing the era name to Tiānlù.
In the eighth month of that year,
Déguāng was buried at Mùyè Shān.
Envoys were sent to Zhènzhōu to summon FÉNG Dào, Hé Níng, and others to attend the funeral.
When the envoys reached Zhènzhōu,
the Zhènzhōu army mutinied,
and General Bái Zàiróng and others expelled Má Dá.
They occupied Dìngzhōu,
and later led all their forces northward.
Má Dá
was Déguāng's cousin.
When Déguāng destroyed Jìn,
he appointed him as the military governor of Xíngzhōu.
When Yuányù was about to ascend,
he ordered him to guard Zhènzhōu.
Má Dá was exceptionally cruel and tyrannical,
often capturing Zhōngguó people,
skinning their faces,
gouging out their eyes,
pulling out their hair,
and severing their wrists before killing them.
When going out or coming in, he always carried tools for pinching, chiseling, gouging, and cutting.
Around his sleeping quarters, human livers, shins, hands, and feet were hung,
yet he spoke and laughed as usual.
The people of Zhèn and Dìng could not endure his poison.
After Má Dá left,
FÉNG Dào and others then returned south.
In the first year of Gānyòu of Hàn,
Wùyù led ten thousand cavalry to attack Xíngzhōu,
capturing Nèiqiū.
When the Qìdān invaded,
they always used horse neighing as a signal.
When they came,
the horses did not neigh,
but spears and halberds shone at night,
and there was also a lunar eclipse.
The barbarian masses were all fearful,
considering it an ill omen.
Although they broke Nèiqiū, more than half of their men and horses were injured or died.
Wùyù reigned for five years.
He convened the chieftains of various tribes
and again plotted an invasion.
The leaders of all tribes were unwilling,
but Wùyù forced them.
Yān Wáng Shùyà and Tàiníng Wáng Òulǐsēng and others led troops to kill Wùyù at Dàshéndiàn.
Déguāng's son, Qí Wáng Shùlǜ, heard of the uprising
and fled to Nánshān.
The Qìdān attacked and killed Shùyà and Òulǐsēng,
and then welcomed Shùlǜ to be enthroned.
Upon Shùlǜ's ascension,
he changed the era name to Yìnglì,
and was styled Tiānshùn Huángdì,
later changing his name to Jǐng.
Shùlǜ suffered from an illness
that prevented him from being intimate with women;
many of his attendants
were eunuchs.
However, he enjoyed hunting and drinking,
and neglected state affairs.
Whenever he drank heavily,
from night until dawn,
he would usually sleep during the day.
The people of the country called him
"the Sleeping King."
Initially,
Wùyù often sent envoys to Hàn.
When the envoy reached Zhōngguó, Zhōu Tàizǔ ascended the throne.
Tàizǔ then sent General Zhū Xiàn to return the diplomatic visit;
Xiàn returned after Wùyù had died.
Upon Shùlǜ's ascension,
he ceased to raid the south.
In the summer of the sixth year of Xiǎndé,
Shìzōng campaigned northward,
appointing Tián Jǐngxián, Military Governor of Bǎodà Commandery, as commander of Yúkǒuguān,
Lǐ Hóngxìn, Right Commander-in-Chief of Shénwǔ, as commander of Héliúkǒu,
Wáng Yàn, former Military Governor of Fèngxiáng, as commander of Yìjīnguān,
and Hán Tōng, Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Guards for Cavalry and Infantry, as overall land forces commander.
Shìzōng himself took a dragon boat from Gānníngjūn,
with a continuous line of covered boats and warships
stretching for dozens of *lǐ* from end to end.
Upon reaching Yìjīnguān,
its defending general surrendered.
As the river path gradually narrowed,
the boats could not proceed,
so he abandoned the boats and traveled by land.
The defending generals of Wǎqiáo Yúkǒuguān, Yíngzhōu, and Mòzhōu
all came forward to surrender.
Just as he was about to order an advance on Yōuzhōu,
Shìzōng fell ill,
so he established Xióngzhōu at Wǎqiáoguān and Bàzhōu at Yìjīnguān, and returned.
The Zhōu army conquered the Three Passes, Yíngzhōu, and Mòzhōu
without bloodshed.
Upon hearing this, Shùlǜ
said to his countrymen:
"These were originally Hàn lands;
now they are returned to Hàn,
so what is there to regret?"
Later, Shùlǜ was killed by a cook during his drunken state.
Alas!
Since ancient times, though the submission and rebellion of the barbarians
did not depend on the rise and fall of Zhōngguó,
Zhōngguó's control over the barbarians invariably depended on its strength or weakness.
I read the Zhōu diary,
and saw Shìzōng take Yíngzhōu and Mòzhōu,
and secure the Three Passes,
without bloodshed.
Yet the historians criticized him for, as a king's army,
rushing a thousand *lǐ* to attack others,
and risking the prestige of the Son of Heaven among reeds and rushes,
in pursuit of a single victory.
Indeed, military strategy
involves seizing opportunities and adapting to circumstances;
there are times that must not be missed.
Shìzōng pacified Huáidiàn in the south,
and campaigned against Qìdān in the north,
capitalizing on his victorious might
to strike when they were bewildered and dispirited.
People only saw how swiftly the Zhōu army moved out,
but did not know that Shùlǜ presented an opportunity that could be seized.
At that time,
Shùlǜ believed that what Zhōu had taken
were all former Hàn territories,
and not worth bothering about.
If so, then the former territories of the Fourteen Prefectures
could all have been commanded and taken.
Unfortunately, Shìzōng fell ill,
and his great ambition was not realized.
However, Yíngzhōu, Mòzhōu, and the Three Passes
were thus able to become people of Zhōngguó again,
while the customs of the Fourteen Prefectures
remain entangled with the barbarians to this day.
How regrettable was his ambition not to be fully achieved,
yet his achievement was not magnificent?
Indeed, the permutations and adaptations of warfare,
how could they be understood by those who rigidly adhere to conventional wisdom!
Initially,
Xiāo Hàn (蕭翰), hearing of Déguāng’s (德光) death,
returned north.
Hú Qiáo (胡嶠), the magistrate of Héyáng (郃陽) County in Tóngzhōu (同州), served as Hàn’s (翰) secretary,
and thus followed him into Qìdān (契丹).
However, Hàn’s (翰) wife, out of jealousy,
accused Hàn (翰) of plotting rebellion.
Hàn (翰) was executed.
Qiáo (嶠), with no one to rely on,
remained among the captives for seven years.
In the third year of Guǎngshùn (廣順) of the Zhōu (周) dynasty,
he escaped and returned to Zhōngguó (中國),
able to relate some of what he had seen.
He said:
“From Yōuzhōu (幽州), heading northwest, one enters Jūyōng Guān (居庸關).
The next day,
again northwest, one enters Shímén Guān (石門關).
The pass road is narrow and steep;
one man can hold off a hundred.
This is the strategic point by which Zhōngguó (中國) controls Qìdān (契丹).
After another three days,
we reached Kèhán Zhōu (可汗州).
To the south, one can see Wǔtái Shān (五臺山);
the highest peak among them
is the East Terrace (Dōngtái 東臺).
After another three days,
we reached Xīnwǔ Zhōu (新武州).
Fifty *lǐ* (里) to the northwest is Jīmíng Shān (雞鳴山).
It is said that Táng (唐) Tàizōng (太宗) heard a rooster crowing here during his northern campaign,
and thus the mountain was named.
The next day,
we entered Yǒngdìng Guān (永定關),
which was an old pass of the Táng (唐) dynasty.
After another four days,
we reached Guīhuà Zhōu (歸化州).
After another three days,
we ascended Tiānlǐng (天嶺).
The ridge stretched continuously east and west.
There was a road leading north down the ridge.
Looking in all four directions, it was a desolate expanse,
with yellow clouds and white grass,
seemingly without end.
The Qìdān (契丹) people said to Qiáo (嶠): ‘This is Cíxiāng Lǐng (辭鄉嶺) [the Ridge of Bidding Farewell to Home];
you may cast one last glance south and say an eternal farewell.’
All those traveling with us wept bitterly,
often fainting and then reviving.
After traveling another three or four days,
we reached Hēiyúlín (黑榆林).
It was July,
but the cold was like deep winter.
The next day,
we entered Xié Gǔ (斜谷).
The valley was fifty *lǐ* (里) long,
with high cliffs and steep gorges.
Looking up, one could not see the sun,
and the cold was even more intense.
After exiting the valley,
we reached flat ground,
and the air became slightly warmer.
After another two days of travel,
we crossed the Huáng Shuǐ (湟水).
The next day,
we crossed the Hēi Shuǐ (黑水).
After another two days,
we reached Tāngchéng Diàn (湯城淀).
The climate there was the warmest.
If the Qìdān (契丹) experienced severe cold,
they would come here for warmth.
Its spring water was clear and cold,
and the grass was soft as down,
suitable for bedding.
There were many exotic flowers;
I recall two types: one called Hàngjīn (旱金),
as large as a palm,
its golden color dazzling;
the other called Qīngnáng (青囊),
like Zhōngguó’s (中國) Golden Lantern (Jīndēng 金燈),
but its color was a lovely blue.
After another two days,
we reached Yíkūn Zhōu (儀坤州) [or Yíkūn Prefecture (儀坤州)],
and crossed the Shèxiāng Hé (麝香河).
From Yōuzhōu (幽州) to this point, there were no distance markers,
and we did not know whether we were heading north or south.
After another two days,
we reached Chìyá (赤崖).
Hàn (翰) and Wùyù (兀欲) caught up with each other,
and then engaged Shùlǜ (述律) in battle at the Shāhé (沙河).
Shùlǜ’s (述律) troops were defeated and fled north.
Wùyù (兀欲) pursued them to Dúshù Dù (獨樹渡),
and then imprisoned Shùlǜ (述律) on Pūmǎ Shān (撲馬山).
After another three days of travel, we reached Shàngjīng (上京),
which was called Xīlóu (西樓).
Xīlóu (西樓) had towns and markets.
Transactions used cloth instead of money.
There were workshops for silk and brocade, eunuchs, Hanlin (Hànlín 翰林) scholars, artisans, performers, wrestlers, scholars, monks, nuns, and Daoist (Dàoshì 道士) priests,
all of whom were Zhōngguó (中國) people,
with those from Bìng (幷), Fén (汾), Yōu (幽), and Jì (薊) being particularly numerous.
Forty *lǐ* (里) east of Shàngjīng (上京),
we reached Zhēnhū Zhài (真珠寨),
where we first ate vegetables.
The next day,
traveling east, the terrain gradually rose.
Looking west, flat pine forests stretched for dozens of *lǐ* (里).
Then we entered a plain,
rich in vegetation.
We first ate watermelons.
It was said that the Qìdān (契丹) obtained these seeds when they defeated the Huíhél (回紇).
They were grown by covering sheds with cow dung,
and were as large as Zhōngguó’s (中國) winter melons but tasted sweet.
Continuing east,
we reached Niǎotán (褭潭).
Willows first appeared here,
and the water and grass were lush and beautiful.
There was a particularly beautiful type of grass called Xījī Cǎo (息雞草).
Its stalks were large;
a horse would be full after eating no more than ten stalks.
From Niǎotán (褭潭), we entered a large mountain range,
traveled for more than ten days, and then exited.
We passed a large forest,
two or three *lǐ* (里) long,
all covered with Wúyí (蕪荑) trees.
Their branches and leaves had thorns like arrow feathers,
and there was no grass on the ground there.
Wùyù (兀欲) set up his tent here at the time,
and assembled the various tribes to bury Déguāng (德光).
From here, we traveled southwest,
sixty *lǐ* (里) a day.
After seven days of travel,
we reached Dàshānmén (大山門).
Two high mountains were about one *lǐ* (里) apart.
There were tall pines and abundant grass,
rare birds and wild flowers.
There were also houses and stone tablets,
which read: ‘This is the imperial tomb.’
Wùyù (兀欲) entered to make offerings.
Among the chieftains of the various tribes, only those carrying sacrificial vessels were allowed to enter.
After they entered, the gate was closed.
The next day the gate was opened,
and they said ‘pāozhǎn’ (拋盞) [throwing cups],
signifying the completion of the ritual.
When asked about the ritual,
they all kept it secret and refused to speak.”
The events Qiáo (嶠) witnessed, such as the imprisonment of Shùlǜ (述律) and the burial of Déguāng (德光),
differ from what is recorded in Zhōngguó (中國) historical accounts.
